title: Auditing and Ethics (Inter P5)
description: CA Intermediate Paper 5 (ICAI new scheme, attempts from May 2027): Standards on Auditing, audit of financial statement items, audit reports and CARO 2020, company audit, bank and entity audits, and professional ethics. Theory-first, with case-based MCQs and 'comment with reasons' practice.

chapters.title: Nature, Objective and Scope of Audit
chapters.summary: What an audit of financial statements is under SA 200, the auditor's overall objectives, reasonable assurance, basic principles and the inherent limitations of an audit.
chapters.lawAsOf: Standards on Auditing issued by ICAI (SA 200) as applicable for the ICAI new scheme Intermediate syllabus

lesson.heading: What an audit is (SA 200)
lesson.body:
An audit of financial statements is an independent examination by a qualified auditor, so that the auditor can express an **opinion** on whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with an **applicable financial reporting framework** (for example, Schedule III with Ind AS or AS for a company).

SA 200 'Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor and the Conduct of an Audit in Accordance with Standards on Auditing' sets two overall objectives:

- To obtain **reasonable assurance** about whether the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, so that the auditor can express an opinion.
- To **report** on the financial statements and communicate as required by the SAs, in accordance with the auditor's findings.

If reasonable assurance cannot be obtained and a qualified opinion is not enough in the circumstances, the auditor disclaims an opinion or withdraws from the engagement where law permits.

**Responsibility split:** management (and those charged with governance) prepare the financial statements and maintain internal control. The auditor's opinion does not relieve management of these responsibilities. This is the premise on which an audit is conducted.

lesson.heading: Reasonable assurance and the key concepts
lesson.body:
**Reasonable assurance** is a high, but not absolute, level of assurance. It is obtained when the auditor has gathered sufficient appropriate audit evidence to reduce **audit risk** (the risk of giving an inappropriate opinion when the statements are materially misstated) to an acceptably low level.

SA 200 requires the auditor to:

- Comply with relevant **ethical requirements**, including independence (ICAI Code of Ethics).
- Plan and perform the audit with **professional skepticism**: a questioning mind, alert to conditions that may indicate misstatement, and a critical assessment of evidence.
- Exercise **professional judgment**: applying training, knowledge and experience to make informed decisions (materiality, audit risk, nature, timing and extent of procedures, evaluating evidence).
- Obtain **sufficient appropriate audit evidence**.
- Comply with all SAs relevant to the audit.

The traditional **basic principles governing an audit** (as taught by ICAI from the earlier AAS 1) are still a useful checklist:

| Principle | Meaning in one line |
| --- | --- |
| Integrity, objectivity and independence | Honest, impartial, free of interest |
| Confidentiality | Client information not disclosed without authority or legal duty |
| Skills and competence | Qualified and up to date |
| Work performed by others | Auditor may use others' work but stays responsible for the opinion |
| Documentation | Record evidence supporting the opinion |
| Planning | Plan for an effective and timely audit |
| Audit evidence | Obtain sufficient appropriate evidence |
| Accounting system and internal control | Understand and evaluate them |
| Audit conclusions and reporting | Review evidence and express a clear opinion |

lesson.heading: Inherent limitations of an audit
lesson.body:
An auditor cannot obtain absolute assurance because of **inherent limitations**. SA 200 groups them as:

- **Nature of financial reporting**: many items involve judgment and estimates (provisions, fair values, useful lives); some uncertainty cannot be removed by any audit procedure.
- **Nature of audit procedures**: management may not give complete information, intentionally or otherwise; fraud may involve collusion, forgery or override of controls designed to conceal it; an audit is not an official investigation and the auditor has no legal power of search.
- **Timeliness and cost-benefit**: the audit must be completed in a reasonable time and at reasonable cost. Difficulty, time or cost alone is not a valid reason to omit a procedure for which there is no alternative.

So most audit evidence is **persuasive rather than conclusive**, and some material misstatements may remain undetected even when the audit is properly planned and performed. That does not by itself show the audit was deficient: adequacy is judged by whether procedures suited the circumstances under the SAs.

lesson.heading: Scope, comparison and qualities
lesson.body:
The **scope** of an audit is set by the applicable law (for companies, the Companies Act 2013 and CARO 2020), the SAs, the terms of engagement (SA 210) and the reporting framework. The client cannot restrict the scope of a statutory audit; a limitation imposed by management affects the opinion.

| Point | Accounting | Auditing | Investigation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Done by | Accountant (management) | Independent auditor | Investigator appointed for a purpose |
| Purpose | Prepare financial statements | Express opinion on them | Find facts on a specific matter |
| Nature | Constructive | Analytical, critical review | Fact-finding, in-depth |
| Period | Current year | Usually one financial year | May cover several years |
| Output | Financial statements | Audit report | Investigation report |

Qualities expected of an auditor: integrity, independence, technical knowledge, tact, alertness, healthy skepticism, sound judgment and good communication.

**Benefits of audit:** credibility of statements for shareholders, lenders and tax authorities; detection of errors and fraud as a by-product; moral check on staff; useful for settling claims, admission or retirement of partners and for valuation.

lesson.heading: Answering 'comment with reasons' questions
lesson.body:
ICAI asks short statements and wants a view plus reasons. A good format is:

- **Provision**: name the SA and paragraph idea (for example, SA 200 on reasonable assurance).
- **Analysis**: apply it to the facts.
- **Conclusion**: 'Hence the statement is correct / not correct'.

**Worked example.** Statement: 'Since the auditor gives an opinion, the audited financial statements are guaranteed to be free from error.'

Answer: Under SA 200 the auditor obtains reasonable, not absolute, assurance because of inherent limitations (judgments in reporting, persuasive evidence, possible collusion and cost-time constraints). The opinion is not a guarantee of accuracy, and management remains responsible for preparation. Hence the statement is not correct.

**Common mistakes:** calling reasonable assurance 'moderate' assurance (that is review engagements); saying the auditor prepares the financial statements; treating detection of fraud as the primary objective; listing limitations without SA 200's three headings.

keyPoints: SA 200: overall objectives are reasonable assurance that FS as a whole are free from material misstatement (fraud or error) and reporting as required by SAs.
Reasonable assurance = high but not absolute; obtained by reducing audit risk to an acceptably low level.
Management prepares FS and maintains internal control; the audit does not relieve them of this.
Professional skepticism (questioning mind) and professional judgment run through the whole audit.
Inherent limitations: nature of financial reporting, nature of audit procedures, timeliness and cost-benefit.
Audit evidence is mostly persuasive, not conclusive.
Cost or difficulty alone is not a reason to skip a procedure with no alternative.

cases.title: Case: Mehta Fabrics Private Limited
cases.body:
CA Riya Kapoor has been appointed statutory auditor of Mehta Fabrics Private Limited for FY 2026-27. At the first meeting, the Managing Director, Mr. Mehta, makes the following remarks:

- 'Your report will certify that every rupee in our books is correct and that no fraud has happened.'
- 'Our accountant left in March. Please prepare the final accounts yourself and then audit them.'
- 'Our stock records are complex. To save time, you may rely on my written confirmation of closing stock of ₹1,85,00,000 and skip the physical verification.'
- 'We do not want you to look into the books of our Surat branch this year.'

Riya's articled assistant suggests that since Mr. Mehta is a respected businessman, his statements should be accepted without further checking.

questions.prompt: Under SA 200, 'reasonable assurance' is best described as:
options: Absolute assurance that the financial statements are free from all errors
A high, but not absolute, level of assurance
A moderate level of assurance, as in a review engagement
No assurance, only a statement of facts found
questions.explanation: SA 200 defines reasonable assurance as a high but not absolute level of assurance. Moderate (limited) assurance applies to review engagements, not audits.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the inherent limitations of an audit listed in SA 200?
options: The nature of financial reporting, involving judgments and estimates
The nature of audit procedures, such as fraud concealed through collusion
The need for the audit to be completed in a reasonable time and at reasonable cost
The absence of the auditor's right to access books of account
questions.explanation: The auditor has a right of access to books (for companies, section 143(1) of the Companies Act 2013). SA 200 lists the other three as inherent limitations.

questions.prompt: An attitude that includes a questioning mind, alertness to conditions indicating possible misstatement and critical assessment of evidence is called:
questions.explanation: This is the SA 200 definition of professional skepticism. Professional judgment is applying training, knowledge and experience to make informed decisions.

questions.prompt: Who is responsible for the preparation of the financial statements of a company?
options: Management, with oversight by those charged with governance
questions.explanation: Preparation and fair presentation, and the internal control needed for it, are management's responsibility. This is a premise on which the audit is conducted under SA 200 and SA 210.

questions.prompt: How should Riya respond to Mr. Mehta's first remark about certifying that every rupee is correct and that no fraud has happened?
options: Agree, because an audit report is a certificate of accuracy
Explain that the audit gives reasonable assurance and an opinion, not a guarantee, due to inherent limitations
Agree only for the fraud part, since fraud detection is the main objective of audit
Refuse to accept the audit because fraud may exist
questions.explanation: Under SA 200 the auditor expresses an opinion based on reasonable assurance. An audit is not a guarantee, and detection of fraud is not the primary objective, though the auditor must respond to fraud risks.

questions.prompt: Regarding the request that Riya prepare the final accounts and then audit them, which is correct?
options: It is acceptable as long as she charges separate fees
Preparation of financial statements is management's responsibility; preparing and auditing them would create a self-review threat and section 144 bars accounting services to the company
It is acceptable for private companies since the Code of Ethics does not apply to them
It is acceptable if the Board passes a resolution
questions.explanation: Management prepares financial statements. Section 144 of the Companies Act 2013 prohibits the company auditor from rendering accounting and book keeping services, and doing so creates a self-review threat under the Code of Ethics.

questions.prompt: Mr. Mehta asks Riya to rely only on his written confirmation of closing stock and skip physical verification. Applying SA 200, the best response is:
options: Accept it, because written representations are conclusive evidence
Accept it, because time and cost justify omitting procedures
Do not accept it; difficulty or cost is not a valid reason to omit a procedure for which there is no alternative, and representations do not replace other evidence
Accept it and mention it in the Other Matter paragraph
questions.explanation: SA 200 says difficulty, time or cost alone is not a valid basis to omit an audit procedure for which there is no alternative. Written representations do not substitute for other audit evidence (SA 580). Attendance at stock count is addressed in SA 501.

questions.prompt: The articled assistant's suggestion that Mr. Mehta's statements be accepted without checking is consistent with professional skepticism.
questions.explanation: Professional skepticism requires the auditor to critically assess evidence regardless of past experience of the honesty and integrity of management. Belief in management's integrity does not reduce the need for evidence.

questions.prompt: Under SA 200, if the auditor cannot obtain reasonable assurance and a qualified opinion is insufficient, the auditor should disclaim an opinion or withdraw where permitted by law.
questions.explanation: SA 200 states this explicitly as the consequence of not achieving the overall objective.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are requirements placed on the auditor by SA 200? (Select all that apply.)
options: Prepare the financial statements if management lacks staff
Comply with all SAs relevant to the audit
questions.explanation: SA 200 requires ethics, skepticism, judgment, sufficient appropriate evidence and compliance with relevant SAs. Preparing financial statements is management's job.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: The Standard on Auditing titled 'Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor and the Conduct of an Audit in Accordance with Standards on Auditing' is SA ___.
questions.explanation: SA 200 is the foundation standard. The 200 series covers general principles and responsibilities.

questions.prompt: State the overall objectives of the auditor under SA 200 and explain the concept of reasonable assurance.
questions.answer:
- SA 200 sets two overall objectives: (a) to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, so that the auditor can express an opinion on whether they are prepared in all material respects in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework; and (b) to report on the financial statements and communicate as required by the SAs.
- Reasonable assurance is a high but not absolute level of assurance.
- It is obtained when sufficient appropriate audit evidence reduces audit risk to an acceptably low level.
- Absolute assurance is not possible due to inherent limitations: the nature of financial reporting (judgments, estimates), the nature of audit procedures (incomplete information, collusion, no power of search) and the need for timeliness at reasonable cost.
- Where reasonable assurance cannot be obtained, the auditor modifies the opinion (disclaimer) or withdraws where law permits.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'The primary responsibility for prevention and detection of fraud rests with the statutory auditor.'
questions.answer:
- Not correct.
- The primary responsibility for prevention and detection of fraud rests with management and those charged with governance, through a strong control environment and internal controls (SA 240).
- The auditor's objective under SA 200 is reasonable assurance that the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.
- Because fraud may involve collusion, forgery and management override, the risk of not detecting a material misstatement from fraud is higher than from error, and an audit cannot guarantee detection.
- The auditor must maintain professional skepticism, identify and respond to fraud risks and report as required (for companies, section 143(12)).
- Hence the statement is incorrect.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'Audit evidence is generally persuasive rather than conclusive.'
questions.answer:
- Correct.
- Under SA 200, inherent limitations mean the auditor draws conclusions from evidence that supports, rather than proves, the assertions in the financial statements.
- Examples: estimates involve judgment; management may withhold information; fraud may be concealed by collusion or forged documents; audit procedures use sampling (SA 530) rather than 100% checking.
- The auditor therefore seeks sufficient appropriate evidence to reduce audit risk to an acceptably low level, giving reasonable rather than absolute assurance.
- Hence the statement is correct.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between auditing and investigation.
questions.answer:
- Objective: audit expresses an opinion on whether the financial statements are prepared in accordance with the framework; investigation establishes facts on a specific matter (for example, suspected fraud or valuation for purchase of a business).
- Scope: audit scope is set by law, SAs and engagement terms; investigation scope is set by the party appointing the investigator.
- Period: audit usually covers one financial year; investigation may cover several years.
- Nature: audit is a general examination, largely on a test basis; investigation is an in-depth, often 100% examination.
- Evidence: audit evidence is mostly persuasive; investigation seeks more conclusive evidence.
- Output: audit report addressed to members; investigation report to the person who commissioned it.
- Timing: audit is often recurring; investigation is done when a need arises.

chapters.title: Audit Strategy, Audit Planning and Audit Programme
chapters.summary: How the auditor sets the overall audit strategy and detailed audit plan under SA 300, writes an audit programme and determines materiality and performance materiality under SA 320.
chapters.lawAsOf: Standards on Auditing issued by ICAI (SA 300, SA 320) as applicable for the ICAI new scheme Intermediate syllabus

lesson.heading: Planning under SA 300
lesson.body:
SA 300 'Planning an Audit of Financial Statements' requires the auditor to plan so that the audit is performed effectively. Planning is **not a discrete phase**: it is a continuous and iterative process that starts after the previous audit ends and continues until the current audit is completed.

**Preliminary engagement activities** at the start of each audit:

- Procedures on continuance of the client relationship and the engagement (SA 220).
- Evaluating compliance with ethical requirements, including independence.
- Establishing an understanding of the terms of the engagement (SA 210).

**Benefits of adequate planning:** attention to important areas; timely identification and resolution of potential problems; a properly organised and managed audit; selection of team members with suitable capabilities; direction, supervision and review of the team; coordination with component auditors and experts.

The **engagement partner and other key members** of the team must be involved in planning, including the team discussion.

lesson.heading: Overall audit strategy vs audit plan
lesson.body:
| Point | Overall audit strategy | Audit plan |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Sets scope, timing and direction of the audit | Converts the strategy into detailed procedures |
| Level | Broad, high level | Detailed |
| Content | Characteristics of engagement (framework, industry reporting, locations); reporting objectives and key dates; significant factors (materiality, high-risk areas, changes); nature, timing and extent of resources | Nature, timing and extent of risk assessment procedures (SA 315), further audit procedures at assertion level (SA 330), other procedures required by SAs |
| Order | Prepared first | Developed after the strategy |

The two are interrelated: a change in one may require a change in the other. Both must be **documented** along with significant changes made during the audit and the reasons (SA 300 and SA 230).

**Initial audit engagements** need extra work: communication with the predecessor auditor (a professional requirement for CAs), review of predecessor working papers where allowed, procedures on opening balances (SA 510) and quality control procedures for accepting the client.

lesson.heading: Audit programme
lesson.body:
An **audit programme** is a detailed, written set of instructions listing the procedures to be performed by the audit team, with space for the staff member's initials, date and working paper reference. It is the practical form of the audit plan.

**Advantages:** clear instructions and division of work; evidence of work done; a basis for reviewing progress; uniformity across years and staff; protection against charges of negligence by showing what was done.

**Disadvantages:** work may become mechanical; staff may not look beyond the programme; may become rigid if not updated for changes in the business; initiative of efficient staff may be curbed.

These disadvantages are overcome by reviewing and updating the programme each year and encouraging staff to report unusual matters.

Extract of an audit programme for purchases:

| Step | Procedure | Done by | W/P ref |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Vouch purchase invoices with GRN and purchase order for 2 sampled months | AK | P-3 |
| 2 | Check GST input credit matches GSTR-2B for sampled invoices | AK | P-4 |
| 3 | Perform cut-off test for invoices 5 days either side of year end | RS | P-6 |

lesson.heading: Materiality under SA 320
lesson.body:
Misstatements are **material** if, individually or in aggregate, they could reasonably be expected to influence the economic decisions of users taken on the basis of the financial statements. Materiality depends on both **size (quantitative)** and **nature (qualitative)** (for example, related party transactions or a breach of a loan covenant can be material even if small).

SA 320 requires the auditor to determine:

- **Materiality for the financial statements as a whole**, when setting the overall audit strategy.
- **Materiality level(s) for particular classes of transactions, account balances or disclosures**, where smaller misstatements could influence users (for example, directors' remuneration).
- **Performance materiality**: an amount set below materiality to reduce to an appropriately low level the probability that aggregate uncorrected and undetected misstatements exceed materiality.

SA 320 does not fix percentages. It suggests **benchmarks**: profit before tax from continuing operations, total revenue, gross profit, total expenses, equity or net assets. Its application material gives examples: about 5% of profit before tax for a profit-oriented manufacturer, about 1% of total revenue or total expenses for a not-for-profit entity.

Materiality is **revised** if information arises during the audit that would have caused a different amount initially. Amounts and factors considered are documented.

lesson.heading: Worked example and common mistakes
lesson.body:
**Example.** Profit before tax from continuing operations is ₹4,80,00,000. The auditor selects 5% as the benchmark percentage and sets performance materiality at 70% of overall materiality.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Overall materiality (5% x 4,80,00,000) | 24,00,000 |
| Performance materiality (70% x 24,00,000) | 16,80,000 |

If PBT is volatile or close to zero, a different benchmark (revenue, normalised profit) may be more appropriate.

**Common mistakes:**

- Treating planning as a one-time step before fieldwork.
- Mixing up strategy (broad direction) and plan (detailed procedures).
- Writing that SA 320 prescribes 5% of profit: it only gives examples; the percentage is professional judgment.
- Ignoring qualitative materiality.
- Forgetting that performance materiality is lower than overall materiality.

keyPoints: SA 300: planning is continuous and iterative, not a discrete phase.
Preliminary engagement activities: continuance (SA 220), ethics and independence, terms of engagement (SA 210).
Overall audit strategy sets scope, timing and direction; audit plan sets nature, timing and extent of procedures.
Audit programme: detailed written instructions; risk of becoming mechanical if not updated.
SA 320: materiality for FS as a whole, for particular items, and performance materiality (lower).
Benchmarks: PBT, revenue, gross profit, total expenses, equity, net assets; percentage is professional judgment.
Materiality has quantitative and qualitative aspects and is revised when new information arises.

cases.title: Case: Sunrise Hotels Limited
cases.body:
M/s Gupta and Associates, Chartered Accountants, are appointed statutory auditors of Sunrise Hotels Limited for FY 2026-27. It is their first year as auditors; the previous auditor completed a five-year term. Extract of draft figures:

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Revenue from operations | 62,00,00,000 |
| Profit before tax (continuing operations) | 3,60,00,000 |
| Total assets | 95,00,00,000 |

The engagement partner CA Neha Gupta decides to use profit before tax as the benchmark and 5% as the percentage, with performance materiality at 75% of overall materiality. The audit manager plans to send the audit plan to the articled assistants without involving the partner or discussing it with the team. During fieldwork, the team learns that the hotel's banquet division (part of continuing operations) will be closed from January 2027, which reduces expected profit sharply.

questions.prompt: According to SA 300, planning an audit is:
options: A discrete phase completed before fieldwork begins
Required only for initial audit engagements
questions.explanation: SA 300 states that planning is not a discrete phase but a continuous and iterative process that often begins shortly after completion of the previous audit.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a matter for the overall audit strategy rather than the detailed audit plan?
options: The sample size for vouching sales invoices
Reporting deadlines and the timing of communications with those charged with governance
The specific confirmation procedures for trade receivables
questions.explanation: Reporting objectives and key dates are part of the overall strategy. Sample sizes and specific procedures belong to the audit plan.

questions.prompt: Performance materiality is:
options: Higher than materiality for the financial statements as a whole
Equal to materiality for the financial statements as a whole
Set below materiality for the financial statements as a whole to reduce aggregation risk
The amount below which misstatements are ignored
questions.explanation: SA 320 defines performance materiality as amounts set by the auditor at less than overall materiality, to reduce the probability that uncorrected and undetected misstatements together exceed materiality.

questions.prompt: A not-for-profit trust has no profit measure. Which benchmark is most suitable for materiality, as illustrated in SA 320?
questions.explanation: SA 320 application material notes that for a not-for-profit entity, a percentage of total revenue or total expenses (around 1%) may be appropriate.

questions.prompt: Using CA Neha Gupta's initial approach, compute performance materiality. Answer in ₹, rounded to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| PBT | 3,60,00,000 |
| Overall materiality (5%) | 18,00,000 |
| Performance materiality (75% of 18,00,000) | 13,50,000 |

questions.prompt: After learning of the banquet division closure that reduces expected profit sharply, what should the auditor do with materiality?
options: Nothing, since materiality is fixed at the planning stage
Revise materiality, as the new information would have caused a different amount initially
Double materiality to save audit time
Report the matter to the Registrar of Companies
questions.explanation: SA 320 requires the auditor to revise materiality if information becomes known during the audit that would have caused a different amount to be determined initially. The auditor also considers whether the strategy and plan need changes.

questions.prompt: The audit manager plans to finalise the plan without the partner and without a team discussion. This is:
options: Acceptable, since planning is the manager's job
Not acceptable; SA 300 requires the engagement partner and other key team members to be involved in planning
Acceptable if the plan is documented
questions.explanation: SA 300 requires the engagement partner and key members of the engagement team to be involved in planning, including the team discussion on susceptibility to material misstatement.

questions.prompt: As this is an initial audit engagement, which additional step is specifically needed?
options: Communicating with the predecessor auditor and performing procedures on opening balances under SA 510
Obtaining a no-objection certificate from the Registrar of Companies
Skipping the risk assessment since the predecessor already did it
questions.explanation: SA 300 lists additional activities for initial engagements, including communication with the predecessor auditor and procedures on opening balances (SA 510).

questions.prompt: SA 320 prescribes that materiality must be 5% of profit before tax for all companies.
questions.explanation: SA 320 gives examples only. The benchmark and percentage are matters of professional judgment.

questions.prompt: A misstatement that is small in amount can still be material because of its nature.
questions.explanation: Materiality has qualitative aspects. For example, a small illegal payment or a misstatement that turns a loss into a profit can be material.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are preliminary engagement activities under SA 300? (Select all that apply.)
options: Performing procedures on continuance of the client relationship
Evaluating compliance with ethical requirements including independence
Establishing an understanding of the terms of the engagement
Sending balance confirmation requests to customers
questions.explanation: SA 300 lists continuance procedures (SA 220), ethics and independence, and terms of engagement (SA 210). Confirmations and reporting happen later.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: The Standard on Auditing dealing with 'Materiality in Planning and Performing an Audit' is SA ___.
questions.explanation: SA 320 covers materiality. SA 450 covers evaluation of misstatements identified during the audit.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the overall audit strategy and the audit plan under SA 300.
questions.answer:
- The overall audit strategy sets the scope, timing and direction of the audit and guides development of the audit plan.
- Strategy considers characteristics of the engagement (framework, industry reporting, locations), reporting objectives and timing, significant factors (materiality, high-risk areas, significant changes) and the nature, timing and extent of resources.
- The audit plan is more detailed: nature, timing and extent of risk assessment procedures (SA 315), further audit procedures at assertion level (SA 330) and other procedures required by SAs.
- Strategy is prepared first; the plan follows, but they are interrelated and updated as the audit progresses.
- Both, and significant changes with reasons, must be documented.

questions.prompt: What is an audit programme? State its advantages and disadvantages.
questions.answer:
- An audit programme is a detailed written plan listing procedures to be performed, with space for initials, dates and working paper references.
- Advantages: clear instructions and allocation of work; record of work done; helps the partner review progress; uniformity of approach; evidence against a charge of negligence; useful guide in later years.
- Disadvantages: work may become mechanical; staff may not look beyond the listed steps; may not suit changed circumstances if not revised; initiative of capable staff may be curbed.
- Remedy: review and update the programme each year, encourage staff to report unusual items and keep it flexible.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'Once materiality is determined at the planning stage, the auditor cannot change it.'
questions.answer:
- Not correct.
- SA 320 requires the auditor to revise materiality for the financial statements as a whole (and for particular items, and performance materiality) if information becomes known during the audit that would have caused a different amount to be determined initially.
- Examples: a decision to dispose of a major part of the business, actual results differing significantly from the draft figures used at planning.
- If materiality is lowered, the auditor considers whether performance materiality and the nature, timing and extent of further procedures remain appropriate.
- The revision and reasons are documented.
- Hence the statement is incorrect.

lesson.heading: Audit risk and its components
lesson.body:
**Audit risk** is the risk that the auditor expresses an inappropriate opinion when the financial statements are materially misstated. It has two parts:

- **Risk of material misstatement (RMM)**: the risk that the statements are materially misstated before the audit. At assertion level it consists of **inherent risk** (susceptibility of an assertion to misstatement before considering controls) and **control risk** (risk that internal control will not prevent, or detect and correct, the misstatement on time).
- **Detection risk**: the risk that the auditor's procedures will not detect a misstatement that exists. Only detection risk is under the auditor's control.

The audit risk model: **Audit risk = Inherent risk x Control risk x Detection risk**.

There is an **inverse relationship** between RMM and acceptable detection risk: the higher the assessed RMM, the lower the detection risk the auditor can accept, so the more persuasive the substantive evidence needed.

**Example.** Acceptable audit risk 5%, inherent risk 80%, control risk 50%. Acceptable detection risk = 0.05 / (0.80 x 0.50) = 0.125, that is 12.5%.

RMM is assessed at two levels: the **financial statement level** (pervasive risks, such as weak tone at the top) and the **assertion level** (specific classes of transactions, balances and disclosures). A **significant risk** is one that requires special audit consideration.

lesson.heading: SA 315: risk assessment procedures and understanding the entity
lesson.body:
SA 315 requires the auditor to identify and assess RMM through understanding the entity and its environment, the applicable financial reporting framework and the entity's system of internal control.

**Risk assessment procedures:**

- Inquiries of management, internal audit and others within the entity.
- Analytical procedures.
- Observation and inspection.

The engagement partner and key team members must **discuss** the susceptibility of the financial statements to material misstatement.

**Components of internal control:**

| Component | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Control environment | Integrity and ethical values, board oversight, HR policies, management philosophy |
| Entity's risk assessment process | How management identifies and responds to business risks |
| Process to monitor the system of internal control | Internal audit, review of controls |
| Information system and communication | Flow of transactions, records, reports, communication of roles |
| Control activities | Authorisation, reconciliations, physical controls, segregation of duties |

**Inherent limitations of internal control:** cost should not exceed benefit; controls target routine transactions; human error; collusion; management override; controls may become outdated.

lesson.heading: Evaluating internal control; internal check and internal audit
lesson.body:
The auditor documents understanding of internal control using:

- **Narrative records**: written descriptions, suited to small entities.
- **Flowcharts**: graphic flow of documents and processes; show segregation of duties clearly.
- **Internal control questionnaire (ICQ)**: questions framed so that a 'No' answer signals a weakness.
- **Checklists**: instructions to be ticked off as completed.

A **walk-through test** traces a few transactions through the system to confirm the understanding.

| Point | Internal check | Internal audit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | Arrangement of duties so one person's work is automatically checked by another | Independent review function within the entity |
| Timing | Continuous, built into processes | Periodic or continuous review after transactions |
| Purpose | Prevent errors and fraud | Evaluate and improve risk management, control and governance |

SA 265 (overview) requires the auditor to communicate **significant deficiencies** in internal control in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis, and other deficiencies to management at an appropriate level.

lesson.heading: SA 330: responding to assessed risks
lesson.body:
**Overall responses** (FS level): emphasising professional skepticism, assigning more experienced staff, more supervision, adding unpredictability in procedures, changing timing (more work at year end).

**Further audit procedures** (assertion level):

- **Tests of controls**: required when the risk assessment expects controls to operate effectively, or when substantive procedures alone cannot give sufficient evidence (for example, highly automated processing). If relying on evidence from previous audits for controls that have not changed, they must be tested **at least once in every third audit**. Controls over a significant risk must be tested in the current period.
- **Substantive procedures**: tests of details and substantive analytical procedures. Irrespective of assessed RMM, the auditor must design and perform substantive procedures for **each material class of transactions, account balance and disclosure**. For a significant risk where only substantive procedures are used, they must include **tests of details**.

Substantive procedures always include agreeing the financial statements with the underlying records and examining material journal entries and adjustments made during preparation.

lesson.heading: Internal control in an IT environment
lesson.body:
Using IT changes how transactions are initiated, recorded and reported, and so changes risks.

| Type | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| General IT controls | Policies supporting the IT environment as a whole | User access management, program change management, data backup and recovery, IT operations |
| Application controls | Controls in a specific application over input, processing and output | Validation checks, sequence checks, three-way match in ERP, exception reports |
| IT-dependent manual controls | Manual controls relying on system reports | Manager reviews an ageing report from the ERP |

**Risks in IT:** unauthorised access and changes to master data; inaccurate processing; loss of data; lack of segregation within systems (super-user rights); dependence on a few IT staff; loss of visible audit trail.

The auditor may use **CAATs** and **data analytics** (for example, testing 100% of journal entries for weekend postings or round-sum entries).

**Common mistakes:** saying the auditor can control inherent or control risk; skipping substantive procedures because controls are strong; confusing internal check with internal audit; forgetting the 'every third audit' rule does not apply to controls over significant risks.

keyPoints: Audit risk = RMM (inherent risk x control risk) x detection risk; only detection risk is controlled by the auditor.
Higher RMM means lower acceptable detection risk and more persuasive substantive evidence.
SA 315 risk assessment procedures: inquiry, analytical procedures, observation and inspection.
Five IC components: control environment, risk assessment process, monitoring, information system and communication, control activities.
SA 330: substantive procedures are mandatory for each material class, balance and disclosure.
Controls relied on from prior audits: test at least once every third audit (not for significant risks).
SA 265: communicate significant deficiencies in writing to those charged with governance.

cases.title: Case: Swift Logistics Limited
cases.body:
CA Arjun Rao is auditing Swift Logistics Limited, which runs its accounting on an ERP system. During the understanding of internal control he notes:

- Ms. Kavita in accounts can create new vendors in the vendor master and can also release vendor payments in the ERP.
- Passwords of the finance team are written on a shared sheet in the accounts office.
- The ERP blocks a purchase invoice from being posted unless it matches the purchase order and goods receipt note (three-way match). Arjun tested this control last year and the IT team confirms no changes this year.
- Revenue from a new government contract involves complex estimates and Arjun has identified it as a significant risk.

Arjun's acceptable audit risk is 4%. He assesses inherent risk for vendor payments at 80% and control risk at 50%.

questions.prompt: Which component of audit risk can be controlled by the auditor?
questions.explanation: Inherent and control risk exist independently of the audit. The auditor manages detection risk by changing the nature, timing and extent of procedures.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a risk assessment procedure under SA 315?
options: Sending external confirmations to all debtors to verify balances
questions.explanation: SA 315 lists inquiry, analytical procedures, and observation and inspection. External confirmation of balances is a substantive procedure (SA 505).

questions.prompt: An internal control questionnaire is usually framed so that:
options: It replaces the need for tests of controls
questions.explanation: ICQs are designed so that a 'No' highlights a weakness to be followed up. They document understanding; they do not test operating effectiveness.

questions.prompt: Under SA 330, substantive procedures for each material class of transactions, account balance and disclosure are:
options: Required only if controls are weak
Required irrespective of the assessed risk of material misstatement
Optional if tests of controls are satisfactory
questions.explanation: Because risk assessment is judgmental and controls have inherent limitations, SA 330 requires substantive procedures for each material item regardless of the assessed RMM.

questions.prompt: Ms. Kavita's ability to both create vendors and release payments is a weakness mainly in:
questions.explanation: Combining master data creation and payment release allows fictitious vendors to be created and paid. This is a segregation of duties failure within control activities, and also an access control (general IT control) weakness.

questions.prompt: Shared passwords written on a sheet are a weakness in which type of control?
questions.explanation: User access management is a general IT control. Weak access controls can undermine all application controls.

questions.prompt: Arjun wants to rely on last year's test of the three-way match control. Which is correct?
options: He may rely on last year's test without any work this year
He must confirm the control has not changed (for example, by inquiry plus observation or inspection) and test it at least once in every third audit
He can never use evidence from previous audits
He must test it only if it relates to a significant risk
questions.explanation: SA 330 allows use of prior-audit evidence for unchanged controls if the auditor establishes continued relevance, and such controls must be tested at least once every third audit. Inquiry alone is not enough to confirm no change.

questions.prompt: Using the audit risk model, compute Arjun's acceptable detection risk for vendor payments. Answer as a % to 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: Detection risk = Audit risk / (Inherent risk x Control risk) = 0.04 / (0.80 x 0.50) = 0.04 / 0.40 = 0.10, that is 10.00%.

questions.prompt: For the revenue on the government contract (a significant risk), if Arjun uses only substantive procedures, they must include tests of details.
questions.explanation: SA 330 requires that where the approach to a significant risk consists only of substantive procedures, those procedures include tests of details.

questions.prompt: Strong internal controls eliminate the need for any substantive procedures.
questions.explanation: SA 330 requires substantive procedures for each material class of transactions, balance and disclosure regardless of the assessed control risk.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are inherent limitations of internal control? (Select all that apply.)
options: Controls usually target routine rather than unusual transactions
The auditor's lack of access to records
questions.explanation: Override, collusion, human error and focus on routine transactions are limitations of internal control. Access to records is a scope matter for the auditor, not a limitation of the entity's controls.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: The risk that a misstatement in an assertion will not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on a timely basis by the entity's internal control is called ___ risk.
questions.explanation: That is control risk. With inherent risk it forms the risk of material misstatement.

questions.prompt: Explain the components of audit risk and the relationship between the risk of material misstatement and detection risk.
questions.answer:
- Audit risk is the risk of expressing an inappropriate opinion on materially misstated financial statements; it is a function of RMM and detection risk.
- RMM exists independently of the audit and has two components at assertion level: inherent risk (susceptibility before controls) and control risk (failure of internal control to prevent or detect and correct).
- Detection risk is the risk that the auditor's procedures fail to detect a material misstatement; it depends on the effectiveness of procedures and their application.
- Audit risk = IR x CR x DR.
- For a given acceptable audit risk, acceptable detection risk is inversely related to RMM: higher RMM requires lower detection risk, so more persuasive evidence through changes in nature (tests of details), timing (closer to year end) and extent (larger samples).

questions.prompt: State the components of internal control under SA 315 with one example each.
questions.answer:
- Control environment: governance and management attitudes, e.g. a code of conduct enforced by the board, independent audit committee.
- Entity's risk assessment process: how management identifies business risks relevant to reporting, e.g. a risk register reviewed quarterly.
- Process to monitor the system of internal control: e.g. internal audit reviews, management review of reconciliations.
- Information system and communication: processes and records for initiating, recording and reporting transactions, e.g. ERP sales module and month-end close calendar.
- Control activities: authorisation, reconciliations, verifications, physical controls and segregation of duties, e.g. bank reconciliation reviewed by the finance manager.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'In a computerised environment the auditor need not consider internal controls because the system processes transactions consistently.'
questions.answer:
- Not correct.
- Consistent processing is a benefit only if the programs and data are correct. An error in a program or master data is repeated in every transaction.
- IT introduces risks such as unauthorised access, unauthorised program changes, loss of data, super-user rights and loss of a visible audit trail.
- Under SA 315 the auditor must understand the information system and the IT environment, including general IT controls (access, change management, operations) and application controls (input, processing, output).
- Where substantive procedures alone cannot provide sufficient evidence in highly automated processing, SA 330 requires tests of controls.
- Hence the statement is incorrect.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between internal check and internal audit.
questions.answer:
- Meaning: internal check is an arrangement of staff duties so that the work of one person is automatically checked by another; internal audit is an independent appraisal function within the organisation.
- Timing: internal check operates simultaneously with recording; internal audit reviews work after it is done (periodic or continuous).
- Object: internal check aims to prevent errors and fraud; internal audit evaluates and improves risk management, control and governance and also detects errors and fraud.
- Staff: internal check uses existing staff through division of work; internal audit uses a separate team or an outsourced firm.
- For companies, section 138 of the Companies Act 2013 requires prescribed classes to appoint an internal auditor; internal check has no such statutory requirement.

chapters.summary: Sufficient appropriate audit evidence (SA 500), specific items (SA 501), external confirmations (SA 505), opening balances (SA 510), audit sampling (SA 530), related parties (SA 550), subsequent events (SA 560), going concern (SA 570) and written representations (SA 580).

lesson.heading: SA 500: sufficient appropriate audit evidence
lesson.body:
**Sufficiency** is the measure of the **quantity** of evidence; **appropriateness** is its **quality**: relevance and reliability. More evidence does not make up for poor quality.

Reliability generalisations (subject to exceptions):

- Evidence from **independent external sources** is more reliable than evidence from the entity.
- Internally generated evidence is more reliable when related **controls are effective**.
- Evidence obtained **directly by the auditor** (observing a control) is more reliable than evidence obtained indirectly or by inference (inquiry about the control).
- **Documentary** evidence is more reliable than oral evidence.
- **Original** documents are more reliable than photocopies, scans or facsimiles.

**Audit procedures to obtain evidence:** inspection, observation, external confirmation, recalculation, reperformance, analytical procedures and inquiry. Inquiry alone is not sufficient.

**Assertions** used by the auditor:

| Classes of transactions | Account balances |
| --- | --- |
| Occurrence | Existence |
| Completeness | Rights and obligations |
| Accuracy | Completeness |
| Cut-off | Accuracy, valuation and allocation |
| Classification | Classification |
| Presentation | Presentation |

If information is to be used as evidence, the auditor considers its relevance and reliability; where it is prepared by a **management's expert**, the auditor evaluates the expert's competence, capabilities and objectivity.

lesson.heading: SA 501 and SA 505: inventory, litigation and confirmations
lesson.body:
**SA 501 Inventory** (when material): attend the physical count unless impracticable, to evaluate management's instructions, observe the count, inspect inventory and perform test counts; then perform procedures on the final inventory records. If attendance is not possible on the planned date due to **unforeseen circumstances**, count on an alternative date and test intervening transactions. If attendance is **impracticable** (for example, location poses safety threats), perform alternative procedures (such as inspecting documents of subsequent sale of specific items acquired before the count); if not possible, modify the opinion under SA 705.

**SA 501 Litigation and claims:** inquiry of management and in-house legal counsel, reviewing minutes and legal expense accounts. If a material risk exists, seek direct communication with the entity's external legal counsel through a letter of inquiry prepared by management and sent by the auditor. If management refuses permission, modify the opinion.

**SA 505 External confirmations:** the auditor maintains **control** over requests (selection, design, sending, receiving).

| Point | Positive confirmation | Negative confirmation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reply needed | Always, agreeing or disagreeing | Only if the respondent disagrees |
| Evidence | More persuasive | Less persuasive |
| Use alone | Generally | Only if RMM is low and controls are effective, population is large with small homogeneous balances, low exception rate is expected and recipients are not likely to disregard |

If **management refuses** to allow a confirmation request: inquire into reasons and seek evidence of their validity, evaluate implications for risk assessment (including fraud), and perform alternative procedures. If the refusal is unreasonable or alternative procedures fail, communicate with those charged with governance and consider the effect on the opinion (SA 705).

lesson.heading: SA 510 opening balances and SA 530 audit sampling
lesson.body:
**SA 510** applies to initial audit engagements. The auditor obtains evidence that opening balances do not contain misstatements that materially affect the current period, that prior period closing balances were correctly brought forward, and that accounting policies are consistently applied. Procedures include reviewing the predecessor auditor's working papers (where permitted) and current period procedures that provide evidence on opening balances. If sufficient evidence cannot be obtained, the auditor expresses a qualified opinion or disclaims, as appropriate.

**SA 530 Audit sampling** means applying procedures to less than 100% of items so that all sampling units have a chance of selection.

- **Sampling risk**: the risk that the conclusion from a sample differs from the conclusion if the whole population were tested.
- **Non-sampling risk**: arises from other factors, such as an inappropriate procedure or misreading evidence.
- **Tolerable misstatement**: the amount the auditor seeks assurance is not exceeded in the population.
- **Anomaly**: a misstatement demonstrably not representative of the population.
- **Stratification**: dividing a population into sub-populations of similar items (for example, by value).

**Selection methods:** random (random numbers), systematic (fixed interval), monetary unit sampling (each rupee has equal chance; larger items more likely selected), haphazard (no conscious bias; not for statistical sampling) and block selection (contiguous items; rarely appropriate).

**Example.** Population of 3,600 sales invoices, sample size 45. Systematic interval = 3,600 / 45 = 80; pick a random start between 1 and 80, then every 80th invoice.

lesson.heading: SA 550, 560, 570 and 580 at a glance
lesson.body:
| SA | Topic | Key requirements |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 550 | Related parties | Understand related party relationships and transactions; remain alert for undisclosed ones (minutes, confirmations, contracts); significant transactions outside normal course are significant risks; evaluate accounting and disclosure (AS 18 / Ind AS 24; section 188 approvals for companies) |
| 560 | Subsequent events | Up to the date of the report: perform procedures to identify events needing adjustment or disclosure. Facts known after report date but before issue: discuss, and if FS amended, extend procedures and give a new or amended report. After issue: if FS amended, new report with an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph referring to the note |
| 570 | Going concern | Evaluate management's assessment covering at least 12 months from the FS date. Indicators: net liability position, loan defaults, negative operating cash flows, loss of key market or management, pending legal proceedings |
| 580 | Written representations | Letter addressed to the auditor, dated as near as practicable to but not after the date of the auditor's report; does not replace other evidence |

**SA 570 reporting:**

| Situation | Opinion |
| --- | --- |
| Basis appropriate, material uncertainty adequately disclosed | Unmodified, with a separate 'Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern' section |
| Material uncertainty not adequately disclosed | Qualified or adverse |
| Going concern basis used but inappropriate | Adverse |

**SA 580:** if management does not provide the representations on its responsibility for preparing the FS and for providing information, or the auditor doubts management's integrity so those are unreliable, the auditor **disclaims** an opinion.

lesson.heading: Exam approach and common mistakes
lesson.body:
For evidence questions, name the SA, list the procedure and state the reporting consequence if evidence is not obtained.

**Worked comment.** 'The auditor may accept management's written representation as sufficient evidence of the existence of inventory.' Not correct: SA 580 says representations do not provide sufficient appropriate evidence on their own. For material inventory, SA 501 requires attendance at the count (or alternative procedures). Representations complement other evidence.

**Common mistakes:**

- Treating sufficiency and appropriateness as the same.
- Saying negative confirmations are always acceptable.
- Dating the representation letter after the audit report.
- Giving an adverse opinion when the material uncertainty is adequately disclosed (it is unmodified with a separate section).
- Using haphazard selection in statistical sampling.

keyPoints: Sufficiency = quantity; appropriateness = relevance and reliability.
External, direct, documentary and original evidence is generally more reliable.
SA 501: attend inventory count when material; letter of inquiry to external legal counsel when risk exists.
SA 505: positive confirmations need a reply; negative only in restricted conditions; management refusal needs inquiry, evaluation and alternative procedures.
SA 530 selection: random, systematic, monetary unit, haphazard, block; interval = population / sample size.
SA 570: material uncertainty adequately disclosed = unmodified opinion plus separate going concern section.
SA 580: representation letter dated near to, but not after, the report date; refusal of key representations leads to disclaimer.

cases.title: Case: Prakash Electricals Limited
cases.body:
CA Meera Iyer is auditing Prakash Electricals Limited for the year ended 31 March 2027. Inventory is ₹14,20,00,000 against total assets of ₹40,00,00,000. Facts noted:

- Heavy rain on 31 March 2027 prevented the team from reaching the warehouse; the stock count was done by management that day.
- Management refuses to let Meera send a balance confirmation to Volt Distributors, the largest customer (balance ₹3,10,00,000), saying the customer is 'sensitive'.
- The company has 3,600 small sales invoices to dealers; Meera plans a sample of 45 using systematic selection.
- The company has defaulted on two loan instalments, and its bankers have not yet agreed to restructure. Management has disclosed this uncertainty in detail in the notes.
- On 20 April 2027, a fire destroyed part of the warehouse. The audit report is planned for 28 May 2027.

questions.prompt: Under SA 500, 'appropriateness' of audit evidence refers to:
options: Whether it is in electronic form
questions.explanation: Appropriateness is the measure of quality: relevance and reliability. Sufficiency is the measure of quantity.

questions.prompt: Which evidence is generally the most reliable?
options: Photocopy of a supplier invoice from the client's file
Bank confirmation received directly by the auditor from the bank
Internal memo prepared by the sales manager
questions.explanation: Evidence from an independent external source obtained directly by the auditor is generally more reliable than internal, oral or copied evidence.

questions.prompt: Which selection method gives each individual rupee in the population an equal chance of selection?
questions.explanation: Monetary unit sampling is value-weighted: each monetary unit has an equal chance, so larger balances are more likely to be selected.

questions.prompt: Written representations under SA 580 should be dated:
options: As near as practicable to, but not after, the date of the auditor's report
Thirty days after the auditor's report
On the date of the annual general meeting
questions.explanation: SA 580 requires this so the representations cover events up to the date of the report.

questions.prompt: Meera could not attend the count on 31 March 2027 due to heavy rain. Under SA 501, she should:
options: Accept management's count sheets as final
Perform or observe some physical counts on an alternative date and test intervening transactions
Give a disclaimer of opinion immediately
Ignore inventory since it is a management responsibility
questions.explanation: When attendance is not possible due to unforeseen circumstances, SA 501 requires counts on an alternative date plus audit procedures on intervening transactions.

questions.prompt: Management refuses the confirmation to Volt Distributors. Which is the correct sequence under SA 505?
options: Accept the refusal and record a note in working papers only

Inquire about reasons and seek evidence of their validity, evaluate implications for risk (including fraud), perform alternative procedures; if unreasonable or unsuccessful, communicate with those charged with governance and consider SA 705
Send the confirmation anyway without management's knowledge
questions.explanation: This is the SA 505 response to a refusal. Alternative procedures may include checking subsequent receipts, shipping documents and sales invoices.

questions.prompt: Compute the sampling interval Meera should use for systematic selection of dealer invoices.
questions.explanation: Sampling interval = population / sample size = 3,600 / 45 = 80. She picks a random start between 1 and 80 and then every 80th invoice.

questions.prompt: Assuming the going concern basis is appropriate and the material uncertainty about loan defaults is adequately disclosed, Meera's report should contain:
options: An unmodified opinion with a separate section headed 'Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern'
questions.explanation: SA 570 requires an unmodified opinion with a separate Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section when disclosure is adequate.

questions.prompt: The fire on 20 April 2027 is an event after the date of the financial statements that Meera must consider under SA 560 before signing her report.
questions.explanation: SA 560 requires procedures to identify events between the date of the financial statements and the date of the auditor's report. A fire after year end is usually a non-adjusting event needing disclosure if material, and it may also affect going concern.

questions.prompt: Negative confirmation requests can be used as the sole substantive procedure for any account balance.
questions.explanation: SA 505 allows negative confirmations as the sole procedure only when all conditions are met: low assessed RMM with effective controls, a large population of small homogeneous balances, a very low expected exception rate, and no reason to believe recipients will disregard them.

questions.prompt: Which of the following may indicate events or conditions casting significant doubt on going concern under SA 570? (Select all that apply.)
options: Loss of a major market or key supplier
Steady growth in operating cash flows
Pending legal proceedings that may result in claims the entity cannot meet
questions.explanation: SA 570 lists financial, operating and other indicators. Growing operating cash flows indicate the opposite.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Under SA 530, a misstatement that is demonstrably not representative of misstatements in the population is called an ___.
questions.explanation: An anomaly is excluded from projection only when the auditor has a high degree of certainty that it is not representative.

questions.prompt: Discuss the auditor's responsibilities under SA 560 for subsequent events at different stages.
questions.answer:
- Events between the date of the financial statements and the date of the auditor's report: the auditor performs procedures to identify all events requiring adjustment or disclosure, such as inquiries of management, reading minutes and latest interim statements, and evaluates their treatment.
- Facts known after the date of the report but before the financial statements are issued: the auditor has no duty to perform procedures, but if a fact becomes known that would have changed the report, discuss with management; if the statements are amended, extend procedures to the amendment and give a new or amended report (with a new date or dual dating). If not amended when needed, the auditor modifies the report or takes steps to prevent reliance.
- Facts known after the financial statements are issued: if amended, review the steps taken to inform users, extend procedures and issue a new report with an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph referring to the note explaining the revision.
- The written representation letter (SA 580) also covers subsequent events.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'Since the inventory count was done by management and certified by the managing director, the auditor need not attend the count.'
questions.answer:
- Not correct.
- SA 501 requires the auditor, where inventory is material, to attend the physical count unless impracticable, to evaluate management's instructions, observe procedures, inspect inventory and perform test counts.
- A certificate from management is a written representation; under SA 580 it does not by itself provide sufficient appropriate evidence.
- If attendance was not possible due to unforeseen circumstances, the auditor counts on an alternative date and tests intervening transactions; if impracticable, alternative procedures are performed.
- If no sufficient evidence is obtained, the auditor modifies the opinion under SA 705.
- Hence the statement is incorrect.

questions.prompt: Explain sampling risk and non-sampling risk under SA 530, and state the methods of sample selection.
questions.answer:
- Sampling risk: the risk that the auditor's conclusion based on a sample differs from the conclusion if the whole population were tested. It may lead to concluding controls are more effective, or misstatement does not exist, when it does (affects effectiveness), or the reverse (affects efficiency).
- Non-sampling risk: the risk of a wrong conclusion for reasons unrelated to sampling, such as an inappropriate procedure or misinterpreting evidence.
- Selection methods: random selection (random number tables or software), systematic selection (fixed interval from a random start), monetary unit sampling (value-weighted), haphazard selection (no conscious bias; not for statistical sampling) and block selection (contiguous items; rarely appropriate).
- The sample must be selected so that each sampling unit has a chance of selection.
