chapters.title: Audit of Items of Financial Statements
chapters.summary: Assertion-based audit procedures for revenue, expenses, assets (PPE, investments, inventory, receivables, cash and bank) and liabilities (share capital, borrowings, payables, provisions and contingent liabilities).
chapters.lawAsOf: Standards on Auditing issued by ICAI; Accounting Standards / Ind AS and Schedule III to the Companies Act 2013 as applicable for the ICAI new scheme Intermediate syllabus

lesson.heading: Approach: start from the assertion
lesson.body:
For every item, ask which assertion carries the highest risk, then pick procedures that address it. Two directions matter:

- **Vouching** (from records to documents) tests **occurrence / existence**: is every recorded item real?
- **Tracing** (from documents to records) tests **completeness**: is every real item recorded?

| Item | Main risk assertion | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Revenue | Occurrence, cut-off | Pressure to overstate profit; fraud risk presumed under SA 240 |
| Expenses and payables | Completeness | Understatement improves profit |
| PPE | Existence, rights, valuation | Capital vs revenue errors; title |
| Inventory | Existence, valuation | Count errors; obsolete stock |
| Receivables | Existence, valuation | Fictitious debtors; doubtful debts |
| Borrowings | Completeness, presentation | Unrecorded loans; current vs non-current |

This table is the backbone of most descriptive answers.

lesson.heading: Revenue and expenses
lesson.body:
**Revenue from operations:**

- Understand the revenue recognition policy (AS 9 or Ind AS 115) and controls over order-to-cash.
- Vouch sales invoices with customer orders, delivery challans / e-way bills and GST returns.
- **Cut-off**: examine invoices and dispatch records a few days either side of year end; check sales returns after year end.
- Analytical procedures: monthly trends, gross margin, comparison with budget and GST turnover.
- Check credit notes and discounts are authorised.

**Expenses:**

- **Purchases**: vouch with purchase order, GRN and invoice (three-way match); check GST input credit; cut-off.
- **Salaries and wages**: compare payroll with attendance and HR records; check for **ghost employees** (no PAN, same bank account for many); recompute PF, ESI and TDS deductions; check payment through bank.
- **Repairs and maintenance**: identify capital items wrongly expensed, and vice versa.
- **Depreciation**: check rates and useful lives per Schedule II, recompute for additions from the date put to use and for disposals up to date of disposal.
- **Rent, insurance**: check agreements and prepaid / outstanding portions.

**Example.** A machine costing ₹24,00,000 was put to use on 1 October 2026; SLM, useful life 10 years, nil residual value. Depreciation for FY 2026-27 = 24,00,000 / 10 x 6/12 = ₹1,20,000. If the company charged ₹2,40,000 (full year), depreciation is overstated by ₹1,20,000.

lesson.heading: Assets
lesson.body:
**Property, plant and equipment:** obtain the fixed asset register and agree to ledger; vouch additions with invoices, board approval and installation certificates; verify **title deeds** of immovable property (CARO 2020 clause 3(i)); physically verify a sample; check disposals and profit or loss on sale; check impairment indicators.

**Investments:** inspect share and demat statements (holding statements from the depository participant), confirm with custodians; check classification (current / non-current) and valuation (AS 13 or Ind AS 109); verify compliance with section 186 for loans and investments by companies.

**Inventory:** attend count (SA 501); check valuation at **lower of cost and net realisable value** (AS 2 / Ind AS 2); test NRV with post year-end selling prices; identify slow-moving and obsolete stock; check stock held with third parties via confirmation; for companies with working capital limits above ₹5 crore secured by current assets, compare quarterly statements filed with banks with books (CARO 2020 clause 3(ii)(b)).

**Trade receivables:** ageing analysis; confirmation (SA 505); subsequent receipts; adequacy of allowance for doubtful debts; Schedule III ageing disclosure.

**Cash and bank:** surprise cash count; bank confirmation directly from banks; check bank reconciliation and clearance of reconciling items after year end; fixed deposits and lien marking.

lesson.heading: Liabilities, provisions and contingent liabilities
lesson.body:
**Share capital:** check memorandum for authorised capital; board and shareholder resolutions for issues; return of allotment filed with the ROC; receipts through bank; share premium; register of members.

**Borrowings:** obtain sanction letters and loan agreements; confirm balances with lenders; check charge creation and satisfaction with the ROC; check interest recompute; classify current maturities of long-term debt as current; check covenant breaches (which may make the loan repayable on demand).

**Trade payables:** completeness is the key risk. Perform a **search for unrecorded liabilities**: examine payments after year end and unprocessed invoices; obtain supplier statements and reconcile; check MSME dues disclosure.

**Provisions and contingent liabilities** (AS 29 / Ind AS 37):

| Situation | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Present obligation, outflow probable, reliable estimate | Provision |
| Possible obligation or outflow not probable | Disclose as contingent liability |
| Outflow remote | No disclosure |

Procedures: inquire of management and lawyers (SA 501), read minutes, review legal expenses, check guarantees given and pending tax demands.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes in answers
lesson.body:
- Writing only 'vouching' for every item without linking to an assertion.
- Testing payables for existence by sending confirmations to listed suppliers only; completeness needs suppliers with nil or small balances and a search for unrecorded liabilities.
- Forgetting cut-off for revenue and purchases.
- Valuing inventory at cost even when NRV is lower.
- Treating every pending lawsuit as a provision.
- Not mentioning the relevant CARO clause or Schedule III disclosure for companies.

**Answer frame** for 'How will you verify X?': 1) understand the policy and controls; 2) existence / occurrence procedures; 3) completeness; 4) valuation and accuracy; 5) rights and obligations; 6) presentation and disclosure (Schedule III, AS / Ind AS, CARO).

keyPoints: Vouching tests occurrence and existence; tracing tests completeness.
Revenue: occurrence and cut-off; SA 240 presumes fraud risk in revenue recognition.
Payables and expenses: completeness; search for unrecorded liabilities through post year-end payments.
Inventory valued at lower of cost and NRV; test NRV with subsequent sale prices.
PPE: verify title deeds (CARO 3(i)); recompute depreciation for additions from date put to use.
Borrowings: sanction letters, confirmation, charges with ROC, current maturities, covenant breaches.
Provision if present obligation, probable outflow and reliable estimate; else contingent liability disclosure unless remote.

cases.title: Case: Greenleaf Agro Products Limited
cases.body:
CA Sanjay Pillai is auditing Greenleaf Agro Products Limited for FY 2026-27. His team notes:

- Sales invoices of ₹42,00,000 dated 30 and 31 March 2027 relate to goods dispatched on 3 April 2027.
- A packing machine costing ₹24,00,000 was put to use on 1 October 2026. The company charged a full year's depreciation of ₹2,40,000 (SLM, 10 years useful life, nil residual value).
- Fertiliser stock costing ₹18,00,000 has expired; it can be sold only as scrap for ₹2,00,000. It is carried at cost.
- A customer has filed a suit for ₹30,00,000 for crop damage. The company's lawyer says it is possible but not probable that the company will lose.
- Payments of ₹11,00,000 made in April 2027 relate to transport services received in March 2027, for which no liability was booked.

questions.prompt: To test the completeness of trade payables, the most effective procedure is:
options: Vouching entries in the payables ledger to invoices
Examining payments made after the year end and unmatched supplier invoices
Sending negative confirmations only to suppliers with large balances
questions.explanation: Completeness is tested by tracing from sources outside the ledger (post year-end payments, unprocessed invoices, supplier statements) to the books. Vouching from the ledger tests existence.

questions.prompt: Which procedure best addresses the existence of trade receivables?
options: External confirmation of balances and checking subsequent receipts
Recomputing the allowance for doubtful debts
questions.explanation: Confirmations from customers (SA 505) and subsequent receipts give evidence that the receivables exist. Ageing and allowances relate mainly to valuation.

questions.prompt: While verifying immovable property of a company, the auditor checks that title deeds are held in the name of the company. This relates to which assertion?
questions.explanation: Title deeds show that the entity holds or controls the rights to the asset. CARO 2020 clause 3(i)(c) also requires reporting on this.

questions.prompt: A sample of employees on the payroll has no PAN, no attendance records and shares the same bank account. This indicates a risk of:
questions.explanation: These are classic red flags for fictitious employees. The auditor should compare payroll with HR records, attendance and statutory filings.

questions.prompt: Sales invoices of ₹42,00,000 dated 30-31 March 2027 for goods dispatched on 3 April 2027 indicate a misstatement in which assertion?
questions.explanation: Revenue has been recorded in the wrong period. The cut-off assertion is breached; FY 2026-27 revenue is overstated and closing inventory understated.

questions.prompt: By how much is depreciation on the packing machine overstated for FY 2026-27? Answer in ₹, rounded to the nearest rupee.
questions.explanation:
| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Correct depreciation: 24,00,000 / 10 x 6/12 | 1,20,000 |
| Depreciation charged | 2,40,000 |
| **Overstatement** | **1,20,000** |

questions.prompt: At what amount should the expired fertiliser stock be carried, and by how much is inventory overstated?
questions.explanation: Inventory is valued at lower of cost (₹18,00,000) and NRV (₹2,00,000), so ₹2,00,000. Carrying it at cost overstates inventory by ₹16,00,000.

questions.prompt: How should the ₹30,00,000 suit be treated, given the lawyer's view?
options: Recognise it as an expense and a provision of 50%
questions.explanation: Outflow is possible but not probable, so no provision is recognised; it is disclosed as a contingent liability under AS 29 / Ind AS 37. The auditor may seek direct communication with the lawyer under SA 501.

questions.prompt: The ₹11,00,000 transport payments in April 2027 would most likely be found by a search for unrecorded liabilities.
questions.explanation: Reviewing payments made after the year end and linking them to the period of service is the standard procedure to detect unrecorded liabilities (completeness).

questions.prompt: Vouching entries from the sales ledger to invoices and dispatch documents primarily tests the completeness of sales.
questions.explanation: Vouching from records to documents tests occurrence. Completeness is tested by tracing from dispatch documents to the sales records.

questions.prompt: Which procedures are relevant when auditing secured term loans of a company? (Select all that apply.)
options: Inspect sanction letters and loan agreements
Check charge creation with the Registrar of Companies
Classify instalments due within 12 months as current maturities
questions.explanation: These address existence, completeness, rights and obligations and presentation of borrowings. Petty cash count is unrelated.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Inventories are valued at the lower of cost and net ___ value.
questions.explanation: AS 2 and Ind AS 2 require the lower of cost and net realisable value.

questions.prompt: How will you verify revenue from sale of goods of a manufacturing company?
questions.answer:
- Understand the revenue recognition policy (AS 9 / Ind AS 115) and evaluate controls over order, dispatch, invoicing and collection.
- Occurrence: vouch a sample of invoices with customer orders, delivery challans, e-way bills and customer acknowledgements; check receipts in bank.
- Completeness: trace dispatch records and gate passes to sales invoices; check sequence of invoice numbers.
- Cut-off: examine dispatches and invoices around the year end; review sales returns and credit notes after year end.
- Accuracy: check prices with approved price lists, discounts with policy, GST computation.
- Analytical procedures: monthly trends, gross margin, comparison with GST returns.
- SA 240 presumes a fraud risk in revenue recognition, so evaluate unusual entries and year-end transactions.
- Presentation: check disclosure under Schedule III.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'Sending confirmations to suppliers with large balances is sufficient to establish the completeness of trade payables.'
questions.answer:
- Not correct.
- The main risk for payables is understatement, so completeness is the key assertion.
- Confirming only large balances tests existence and accuracy of what is recorded; it does not find liabilities that are not recorded.
- For completeness the auditor should also select suppliers with nil or small balances and regular suppliers, reconcile supplier statements, examine payments after year end and unprocessed invoices and GRNs not invoiced (search for unrecorded liabilities).
- The auditor also checks MSME dues disclosure under Schedule III.
- Hence the statement is incorrect.

questions.prompt: How will you verify contingent liabilities of a company?
questions.answer:
- Understand the requirements of AS 29 / Ind AS 37: provision vs contingent liability vs remote.
- Inquire of management and in-house counsel; obtain a list of pending suits, claims, guarantees and tax demands.
- Read board and committee minutes, correspondence with lawyers and legal expense ledgers.
- Where material litigation risk exists, send a letter of inquiry to external legal counsel under SA 501.
- Examine guarantees given, letters of credit and bills discounted with bank confirmations.
- Check post year-end events (SA 560) for settlements.
- Obtain written representations (SA 580) that all known contingent liabilities are disclosed.
- Verify disclosure in the notes as per Schedule III.

chapters.title: Audit Documentation and Analytical Procedures
chapters.summary: What audit documentation must contain under SA 230, assembly, retention and ownership of working papers, analytical procedures under SA 520 and an overview of evaluating misstatements under SA 450.
chapters.lawAsOf: Standards on Auditing issued by ICAI (SA 230, SA 520, SA 450 overview) and SQC 1 (SQM 1 deferred by ICAI in 2026) as applicable for the ICAI new scheme Intermediate syllabus

lesson.heading: SA 230: purpose and content of audit documentation
lesson.body:
**Audit documentation** is the record of audit procedures performed, relevant audit evidence obtained and conclusions reached ('working papers'). It provides:

- Evidence of the basis for the auditor's conclusion about achieving the overall objectives.
- Evidence that the audit was planned and performed in accordance with SAs and legal requirements.

It also helps the team plan and perform the audit, supervise and review, keep accountability, retain matters of continuing significance, and enables quality reviews and inspections.

**Standard for form, content and extent:** documentation must be sufficient to enable an **experienced auditor, having no previous connection with the audit**, to understand:

- The nature, timing and extent of procedures performed.
- The results of the procedures and the evidence obtained.
- Significant matters arising, conclusions reached and significant professional judgments made.

The auditor records the **identifying characteristics** of items tested, **who performed** the work and the date, and **who reviewed** it, the date and extent of review. Discussions of significant matters with management and TCWG are documented. If the auditor departs from a relevant requirement, he documents how alternative procedures achieved the aim of that requirement.

Form depends on size and complexity: paper, electronic or other media. Documentation is **not** required for superseded drafts or notes reflecting incomplete thinking.

lesson.heading: Assembly, retention, ownership and custody
lesson.body:
| Point | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Assembly of final file | Complete the administrative process on a timely basis after the report date. SQC 1 sets an appropriate time limit of not more than **60 days** after the date of the auditor's report |
| After assembly | Do not delete or discard documentation before the end of the retention period. Any modification or addition must record the reasons, when and by whom it was made and reviewed |
| Retention period | SQC 1: not shorter than **seven years** from the date of the auditor's report (or later, if law requires) |
| Ownership | Working papers are the **property of the auditor** |
| Access by client | The auditor may, at his discretion, make portions available to the entity, provided it does not undermine independence or the validity of the engagement |
| Custody | Firm must have policies for confidentiality, safe custody, integrity, accessibility and retrievability |

After the report date, if exceptional circumstances require new procedures or conclusions, the auditor documents the circumstances, the new procedures, evidence, conclusions and their effect on the report, and when and by whom changes were made and reviewed.

Note: ICAI issued SQM 1 and SQM 2 to replace SQC 1, but in 2026 the ICAI Council deferred their mandatory effective date; SQC 1 continues to apply until a further announcement. Check the latest ICAI announcement before your attempt.

**Permanent file vs current file:**

| Permanent audit file | Current audit file |
| --- | --- |
| Matters of continuing importance: MOA and AOA, organisation chart, important agreements, accounting policies, internal control notes, previous years' analytical data | Matters for this year: audit plan and programme, engagement letter, working papers on each item, representation letter, TCWG communication, draft financial statements |

lesson.heading: SA 520: analytical procedures
lesson.body:
**Analytical procedures** are evaluations of financial information through analysis of plausible relationships among financial and non-financial data, including investigation of fluctuations that are inconsistent with other information or differ significantly from expected values.

They are used at three stages:

| Stage | Standard | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Planning | SA 315 | Risk assessment procedure: identify unusual changes |
| Fieldwork | SA 520 | Substantive analytical procedure for an assertion |
| Near the end | SA 520 | Mandatory overall review: are the FS consistent with the auditor's understanding? |

When designing **substantive analytical procedures**, the auditor must:

- Determine their suitability for the assertion (best for large volumes of predictable transactions).
- Evaluate the **reliability of data** used to develop the expectation (source, comparability, nature, relevance, controls over preparation).
- Develop an **expectation** precise enough to identify a material misstatement.
- Determine the amount of difference from expectation that is acceptable without further investigation.

If fluctuations are inconsistent or unexpected, the auditor **inquires of management** and **corroborates** the responses with other evidence, and performs other procedures as needed.

Techniques: **ratio analysis** (gross margin, inventory turnover, debtor days), **trend analysis** (month on month), **reasonableness tests** (build an independent expectation).

lesson.heading: Worked reasonableness test and SA 450 overview
lesson.body:
**Example: interest income on fixed deposits.** The company holds fixed deposits of ₹2,50,00,000 throughout the year at 7% per annum.

| Particulars | ₹ |
| --- | --- |
| Expected interest (2,50,00,000 x 7%) | 17,50,000 |
| Interest recorded | 15,10,000 |
| Difference | 2,40,000 |

If ₹2,40,000 exceeds the acceptable threshold, the auditor asks management and corroborates (for example, with bank interest certificates and Form 26AS); a likely cause is unrecorded accrued interest at year end.

**SA 450 'Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit' (overview):**

- Accumulate misstatements identified, other than those that are **clearly trivial**.
- Communicate them on a timely basis to the appropriate level of management and request correction.
- If management refuses to correct some, obtain the reasons and consider them when evaluating whether the FS as a whole are free from material misstatement.
- Reassess materiality (SA 320) before evaluating the effect of uncorrected misstatements.
- Communicate uncorrected misstatements to TCWG and request a **written representation** that management believes their effects are immaterial (a summary is attached to the representation letter).
- Document the amount below which misstatements are clearly trivial, all misstatements accumulated and whether corrected, and the auditor's conclusion.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Saying the client owns working papers because it paid the audit fee.
- Saying working papers must be handed to the client on demand. They may be shared at the auditor's discretion only.
- Writing 'documentation must include all drafts'. Superseded drafts are not required.
- Treating analytical procedures as optional at the final stage. SA 520 requires them near the end of the audit to form an overall conclusion.
- Accepting management's explanation for a fluctuation without corroboration.
- Mixing retention (seven years) and assembly (60 days).

keyPoints: SA 230 test: an experienced auditor with no previous connection must understand procedures, results, evidence and significant judgments.
Record identifying characteristics, preparer and date, reviewer, date and extent of review.
Assemble final file within 60 days of the report date (SQC 1); retain at least seven years.
Working papers belong to the auditor; client access only at the auditor's discretion.
SA 520: suitability, reliability of data, precise expectation, acceptable difference; analytical review near the end is mandatory.
Unexpected fluctuations: inquire of management and corroborate.
SA 450: accumulate misstatements other than clearly trivial; request correction; written representation on uncorrected misstatements.

cases.title: Case: Bright Pharma Limited
cases.body:
CA Farhan Sheikh signed the audit report of Bright Pharma Limited for FY 2026-27 on 15 May 2027. Facts:

- The final audit file was assembled on 25 August 2027.
- In October 2027 the company's new CFO demanded the complete set of working papers, saying 'the company paid for the audit, so the papers belong to us'.
- Farhan's office manager proposes to destroy all FY 2026-27 working papers in 2030 to free storage space.
- During the audit, gross margin rose from 32% to 41% with no change in product mix or prices. The CFO explained it as 'better efficiency'. The team accepted the explanation and recorded only 'explained by management' in the file.
- The team identified misstatements totalling ₹6,50,000; management corrected ₹4,00,000 and refused to correct the rest.

questions.prompt: Under SA 230, audit documentation should be sufficient to enable whom to understand the work performed?
options: An experienced auditor having no previous connection with the audit
questions.explanation: This is the SA 230 benchmark for form, content and extent of documentation.

questions.prompt: Which of the following need NOT be included in audit documentation?
options: Who reviewed the work and when
Superseded drafts of working papers and notes reflecting incomplete thinking
questions.explanation: SA 230 states that superseded drafts, notes on incomplete or preliminary thinking and copies of corrected documents need not be included.

questions.prompt: Analytical procedures near the end of the audit under SA 520 are:
options: Required, to form an overall conclusion on whether the FS are consistent with the auditor's understanding of the entity
questions.explanation: SA 520 requires the auditor to design and perform analytical procedures near the end of the audit to assist in forming an overall conclusion.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would normally be kept in the permanent audit file?
options: Bank reconciliation for the current year
questions.explanation: The permanent file holds documents of continuing importance such as the MOA, AOA and long-term agreements. The others are current file items.

questions.prompt: Farhan assembled the final file on 25 August 2027. Under SQC 1, the appropriate time limit for completing assembly was:
options: Not more than 30 days after the report date, so he was late
Not more than 60 days after the report date, so he was late
Not more than 120 days after the report date, so he was on time
questions.explanation: SQC 1 sets not more than 60 days after the date of the auditor's report. 15 May plus 60 days is 14 July 2027, so 25 August is late.

questions.prompt: The CFO's claim that working papers belong to the company is:
options: Correct, as the company paid the audit fee
Incorrect; working papers are the property of the auditor, who may at his discretion make portions available to the entity
questions.explanation: SA 230 read with SQC 1: documentation is the property of the auditor. Sharing portions is at the auditor's discretion if it does not undermine independence or the validity of the work.

questions.prompt: The office manager's plan to destroy FY 2026-27 working papers in 2030 is:
options: Acceptable, as three years is enough
Not acceptable; they must be retained for at least seven years from the date of the auditor's report
Acceptable if scanned copies are not kept
questions.explanation: SQC 1 requires retention of engagement documentation for not less than seven years from the date of the auditor's report, longer if law requires.

questions.prompt: Accepting the CFO's 'better efficiency' explanation for the jump in gross margin without corroboration complies with SA 520.
questions.explanation: SA 520 requires inquiry of management and corroboration of the response with other evidence. A 9-point margin jump with no price or mix change is a red flag for misstatement, such as overstated closing inventory or revenue.

questions.prompt: What is the amount of uncorrected misstatements Farhan must evaluate and communicate under SA 450? Answer in ₹.
questions.explanation: Uncorrected = identified 6,50,000 - corrected 4,00,000 = ₹2,50,000. He obtains reasons for non-correction, evaluates the effect on the FS as a whole, communicates to TCWG and obtains a written representation.

questions.prompt: After the final audit file is assembled, the auditor may delete working papers he considers unnecessary before the retention period ends.
questions.explanation: SA 230 prohibits deleting or discarding documentation of any nature after assembly and before the end of the retention period.

questions.prompt: When designing substantive analytical procedures, SA 520 requires the auditor to: (Select all that apply.)
options: Determine the suitability of the procedure for the assertion
Evaluate the reliability of data used to develop the expectation
Develop an expectation precise enough to identify a material misstatement
Determine the acceptable difference without further investigation
Obtain approval of the expectation from management
questions.explanation: These are the four SA 520 design requirements. Management does not approve the auditor's expectations.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Under SA 450, the auditor accumulates misstatements identified during the audit, other than those that are clearly ___.
questions.explanation: Clearly trivial misstatements are of a wholly different, smaller order than materiality and need not be accumulated.

questions.prompt: Explain the form, content and extent of audit documentation under SA 230.
questions.answer:
- Documentation must enable an experienced auditor with no previous connection with the audit to understand: the nature, timing and extent of procedures performed; the results and evidence obtained; and significant matters, conclusions and significant professional judgments.
- Form and extent depend on the size and complexity of the entity, nature of procedures, identified risks, significance of evidence, nature of exceptions and the audit methodology and tools used.
- The auditor records identifying characteristics of items tested, who performed the work and when, and who reviewed it, when and to what extent.
- Discussions of significant matters with management and TCWG are recorded, including when and with whom.
- Inconsistencies with a final conclusion on a significant matter and how they were addressed are recorded.
- Departures from relevant requirements and alternative procedures are documented.
- Superseded drafts and preliminary notes need not be retained.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'Working papers are the property of the client and must be handed over on demand.'
questions.answer:
- Not correct.
- Under SA 230 read with SQC 1, audit documentation is the property of the auditor.
- The auditor may, at his discretion, make portions of or extracts from documentation available to the client, provided this does not undermine the validity of the work or the independence of the auditor or his personnel.
- The auditor must keep documentation confidential and in safe custody, and retain it for at least seven years from the date of the report.
- Disclosure to third parties needs client consent unless required by law or professional duty (Code of Ethics, confidentiality).
- Hence the statement is incorrect.

questions.prompt: What are analytical procedures? Explain their use at different stages of the audit.
questions.answer:
- Analytical procedures are evaluations of financial information through analysis of plausible relationships among financial and non-financial data, including investigation of unexpected fluctuations (SA 520).
- Planning stage (SA 315): as a risk assessment procedure, to identify unusual transactions, ratios and trends that may indicate risks of material misstatement.
- Substantive stage (SA 520): as substantive procedures where relationships are predictable, after considering suitability, reliability of data, precision of expectation and acceptable difference.
- Final stage (SA 520, mandatory): an overall review to conclude whether the financial statements are consistent with the auditor's understanding of the entity.
- Unexpected results are investigated through inquiry of management, corroboration and other procedures.
- Techniques: ratio analysis, trend analysis and reasonableness tests.

chapters.title: Audit Report (SA 700, 701, 705, 706) and CARO 2020
chapters.summary: Forming an opinion and the structure of the auditor's report, key audit matters, modified opinions, Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter paragraphs, and the applicability and main clauses of CARO 2020.
chapters.lawAsOf: Standards on Auditing issued by ICAI (SA 700, 701, 705, 706); Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 under section 143(11) of the Companies Act 2013, as applicable for the ICAI new scheme Intermediate syllabus

lesson.heading: SA 700: forming the opinion and the report
lesson.body:
The auditor forms an opinion on whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework. He concludes whether reasonable assurance has been obtained, considering whether sufficient appropriate evidence was obtained (SA 330), whether uncorrected misstatements are material (SA 450) and the qualitative aspects of accounting practices.

An **unmodified opinion** is expressed when the auditor concludes the FS are prepared in all material respects in accordance with the framework.

**Elements of the auditor's report (in order for a company audit):**

| Element | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Title | 'Independent Auditor's Report' |
| Addressee | Members of the company |
| Opinion | First section, headed 'Opinion' |
| Basis for Opinion | Audit conducted per SAs; independence; evidence sufficient and appropriate |
| Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern | Only if applicable (SA 570) |
| Key Audit Matters | Listed entities (SA 701) |
| Other Information | SA 720 (for example, board's report) |
| Responsibilities of management and TCWG | Preparation, internal control, going concern assessment |
| Auditor's responsibilities | Reasonable assurance, skepticism, risk assessment |
| Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements | Section 143(3) matters, CARO 2020 annexure, internal financial controls annexure |
| Signature, membership number, place, date, UDIN | Date not earlier than the date the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate evidence, including that FS are approved |

lesson.heading: SA 705: modified opinions
lesson.body:
A modification is needed when (a) the FS as a whole are materially misstated, or (b) the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. The type depends on the **nature** of the matter and how **pervasive** its effects are.

| Nature of matter | Material but not pervasive | Material and pervasive |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FS are materially misstated | Qualified opinion | Adverse opinion |
| Unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence | Qualified opinion | Disclaimer of opinion |

**Pervasive** effects are not confined to specific elements, or if confined, represent a substantial part of the FS, or relate to disclosures fundamental to users' understanding.

When the opinion is modified, the 'Basis for Opinion' heading becomes 'Basis for Qualified / Adverse / Disclaimer of Opinion' and describes the matter, quantifying the financial effect where practicable.

**Limitation imposed by management:** if, after accepting the engagement, management imposes a scope limitation likely to lead to a qualified opinion or disclaimer, the auditor requests removal; if refused, communicates with TCWG, performs alternative procedures and, if needed, qualifies, disclaims or withdraws where possible and permitted by law.

In a disclaimer, the auditor does not report KAM (except as required) and states that he does not express an opinion.

lesson.heading: SA 701 KAM and SA 706 EOM / Other Matter
lesson.body:
**Key Audit Matters (SA 701):** matters that, in the auditor's professional judgment, were of **most significance** in the audit of the current period. They are selected from matters communicated with TCWG, considering:

- Areas of higher assessed RMM or significant risks.
- Significant auditor judgments relating to areas of significant management judgment, including estimates with high uncertainty.
- Effect of significant events or transactions during the period.

KAM is required for audits of **listed entities**, and when the auditor decides or law requires. KAM is **not** a substitute for a modified opinion or for the going concern material uncertainty section. A matter giving rise to a modified opinion is reported in the Basis for Opinion section, not as KAM.

**Emphasis of Matter (SA 706):** draws attention to a matter **appropriately presented or disclosed** in the FS that is **fundamental** to users' understanding. Not used if the matter is a KAM. Examples: uncertainty about the outcome of exceptional litigation, a major catastrophe with significant effect, early application of a new accounting standard with pervasive effect.

**Other Matter paragraph (SA 706):** refers to a matter **not presented or disclosed** in the FS that is relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or report. Example: FS of a prior period audited by another auditor (SA 710), or restriction on distribution of the report.

| Point | EOM | Other Matter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Matter in FS? | Yes, appropriately disclosed | No |
| Purpose | Highlight fundamental disclosure | Explain audit or report |
| Effect on opinion | None; 'Our opinion is not modified' | None |

lesson.heading: CARO 2020 basics
lesson.body:
The Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 is issued by the Central Government under **section 143(11)**. It applies to audits of financial statements for financial years beginning on or after **1 April 2021**, and the auditor reports on the matters in **paragraph 3** (21 clauses) in an annexure to the audit report.

**Not applicable to:**

- A banking company.
- An insurance company.
- A company licensed under section 8 (not-for-profit).
- A One Person Company.
- A small company as defined in section 2(85).
- A private limited company, not a holding or subsidiary of a public company, with paid-up capital and reserves and surplus not more than **₹1 crore** as on the balance sheet date, total borrowings from banks or financial institutions not more than **₹1 crore** at any point during the year, and total revenue (including from discontinued operations) not more than **₹10 crore** during the year. All conditions must be met.

CARO does not apply to the auditor's report on **consolidated** FS, except clause 3(xxi).

**Selected clauses:**

| Clause | Matter |
| --- | --- |
| 3(i) | PPE records, physical verification, title deeds of immovable property |
| 3(ii) | Physical verification of inventory; quarterly statements to banks for working capital limits above ₹5 crore |
| 3(iv) | Compliance with sections 185 and 186 for loans, investments, guarantees |
| 3(vii) | Regularity in depositing undisputed statutory dues; disputed dues not deposited |
| 3(ix) | Default in repayment of loans; diversion of term loans |
| 3(xi) | Fraud noticed or reported; whistle-blower complaints |
| 3(xiii) | Compliance with sections 177 and 188 for related party transactions |
| 3(xvii) | Cash losses in current and previous year |
| 3(xviii) | Resignation of statutory auditors |
| 3(xix) | Material uncertainty on meeting liabilities within one year |
| 3(xx) | Unspent CSR amount transfers |
| 3(xxi) | Qualifications or adverse remarks in CARO reports of companies included in consolidated FS |

Under **paragraph 4**, where an answer is unfavourable or qualified, the auditor states the reasons.

lesson.heading: Exam technique and common mistakes
lesson.body:
For opinion questions, use a three-step frame: (1) is the matter a misstatement or a scope limitation? (2) is it material? (3) is it pervasive? Then name the opinion and the section where the matter is described.

**Worked example.** A company has not provided for gratuity of ₹40,00,000 (material, confined to one item, profit still positive). The FS are misstated, material but not pervasive: **qualified opinion**, described in 'Basis for Qualified Opinion', with the effect on profit and liabilities.

**Common mistakes:**

- Using EOM to report a misstatement (EOM is only for matters properly disclosed).
- Giving an adverse opinion for a scope limitation (scope limitation leads to qualified or disclaimer).
- Putting a qualification matter in the KAM section.
- Saying CARO applies to all private companies; check the three ₹1 crore / ₹1 crore / ₹10 crore conditions.
- Forgetting that the Opinion section comes first in the report.

keyPoints: SA 700: Opinion section comes first, followed by Basis for Opinion.
SA 705: misstatement gives qualified (material) or adverse (pervasive); scope limitation gives qualified or disclaimer (pervasive).
SA 701: KAM required for listed entities; not a substitute for modified opinion or going concern section.
SA 706: EOM for matters properly disclosed and fundamental; Other Matter for matters not in the FS.
CARO 2020 under section 143(11): 21 clauses in paragraph 3; applies for FY beginning on or after 1 April 2021.
CARO exempt: banking, insurance, section 8, OPC, small companies, and private companies meeting all of the ₹1 crore capital, ₹1 crore borrowings and ₹10 crore revenue limits.
CARO does not apply to consolidated FS except clause 3(xxi).

cases.title: Case: Orion Textiles Limited
cases.body:
CA Pooja Nair is the auditor of Orion Textiles Limited, a listed company, for FY 2026-27. Profit before tax is ₹12,00,00,000 and materiality is ₹60,00,000. Findings:

- Trade receivables include ₹1,10,00,000 due from a customer that went into liquidation in February 2027. Management refuses to provide for it. Other balances are fine.
- A flood in May 2027 damaged one of the four plants. The company has fully and properly disclosed the event and its expected effect in the notes.
- Valuation of inventory involves complex judgments about obsolescence and was the area that took the most audit effort; it was discussed in detail with the audit committee. Pooja is satisfied with the valuation.
- The previous year's financial statements were audited by another firm, which expressed an unmodified opinion.

questions.prompt: When the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and the possible effects are material and pervasive, the opinion is:
questions.explanation: SA 705: scope limitation with material and pervasive possible effects leads to a disclaimer. Adverse is for material and pervasive misstatements.

questions.prompt: In the auditor's report under SA 700, which section appears first?
questions.explanation: SA 700 requires the Opinion section to be the first section, followed immediately by the Basis for Opinion section.

questions.prompt: CARO 2020 is issued under which section of the Companies Act 2013?
questions.explanation: Section 143(11) empowers the Central Government to direct that the auditor's report include a statement on prescribed matters. CARO 2020 is that order.

questions.prompt: A private company (not a holding or subsidiary of a public company) has paid-up capital and reserves of ₹80 lakh, maximum bank borrowings of ₹1.4 crore during the year and revenue of ₹6 crore. Is CARO 2020 applicable?
options: No, because capital and reserves are below ₹1 crore
Yes, because borrowings exceeded ₹1 crore at some point during the year
No, because revenue is below ₹10 crore
Yes, CARO applies to every private company
questions.explanation: The private company exemption needs all three conditions. Borrowings above ₹1 crore at any point during the year break the exemption, so CARO applies (assuming it is not a small company).

questions.prompt: What opinion should Pooja express on the non-provision of ₹1,10,00,000 against the liquidated customer?
options: Unmodified, with an Emphasis of Matter
Qualified opinion, as the misstatement is material but not pervasive
questions.explanation: ₹1.10 crore exceeds materiality of ₹60 lakh, so it is material, but it is confined to one balance and profit remains substantial, so it is not pervasive. SA 705 gives a qualified opinion.

questions.prompt: How should the properly disclosed flood damage be reflected in the report, if Pooja considers it fundamental to users' understanding?
questions.explanation: A major catastrophe that is properly disclosed and fundamental to users' understanding is a typical SA 706 Emphasis of Matter example. The opinion is not modified for it.

questions.prompt: Inventory valuation, which took the most audit effort and was discussed with the audit committee, is best reported as:
options: A Key Audit Matter under SA 701
questions.explanation: It was of most significance, involved significant judgment and was communicated with TCWG. For a listed company it is reported as a KAM. Since Pooja is satisfied, it is not a qualification.

questions.prompt: The fact that the prior year's financial statements were audited by another auditor is reported in:
options: The Basis for Qualified Opinion section
questions.explanation: Under SA 710 read with SA 706, where prior period FS were audited by a predecessor auditor, the auditor may state this, with the type of opinion expressed, in an Other Matter paragraph.

questions.prompt: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph can be used instead of qualifying the opinion when the auditor disagrees with management's accounting treatment.
questions.explanation: SA 706 states that an EOM is not a substitute for a modified opinion. EOM applies only to matters appropriately presented or disclosed.

questions.prompt: CARO 2020 does not apply to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements except for clause 3(xxi).
questions.explanation: Clause 3(xxi) requires reporting of qualifications or adverse remarks in the CARO reports of companies included in the consolidated FS.

questions.prompt: To which of the following is CARO 2020 NOT applicable? (Select all that apply.)
questions.explanation: CARO 2020 exempts banking, insurance, section 8 companies, OPCs, small companies and qualifying private companies. A listed company is covered.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: The Standard on Auditing on 'Communicating Key Audit Matters in the Independent Auditor's Report' is SA ___.
questions.explanation: SA 701 deals with KAM. SA 705 deals with modified opinions and SA 706 with EOM and Other Matter paragraphs.

questions.prompt: Explain the circumstances in which an auditor modifies the opinion and the types of modified opinion under SA 705.
questions.answer:
- The auditor modifies the opinion when (a) he concludes, based on evidence obtained, that the FS as a whole are not free from material misstatement, or (b) he is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence to conclude that the FS as a whole are free from material misstatement.
- Qualified opinion: misstatements are material but not pervasive; or, for a scope limitation, possible effects could be material but not pervasive.
- Adverse opinion: misstatements are both material and pervasive.
- Disclaimer of opinion: unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and possible effects of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive.
- Pervasive effects are not confined to specific elements, or represent a substantial proportion, or relate to fundamental disclosures.
- The Basis for Opinion section is retitled and describes and quantifies the matter where practicable.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between an Emphasis of Matter paragraph and an Other Matter paragraph under SA 706.
questions.answer:
- EOM refers to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed in the FS that, in the auditor's judgment, is fundamental to users' understanding of the FS.
- Other Matter paragraph refers to a matter not presented or disclosed in the FS that is relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the report.
- Examples of EOM: uncertainty about exceptional litigation, a major catastrophe, early application of a new standard. Examples of Other Matter: prior period FS audited by another auditor, restriction on distribution of the report.
- Neither modifies the opinion; EOM states that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter.
- EOM is not used for a matter already reported as KAM, and neither is a substitute for a modified opinion or for SA 570 reporting.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'Key Audit Matters may be reported in place of a qualified opinion to soften the auditor's report.'
questions.answer:
- Not correct.
- SA 701 states that communicating KAM is not a substitute for: disclosures required in the FS; a modified opinion under SA 705; or reporting a material uncertainty on going concern under SA 570.
- A matter giving rise to a qualified or adverse opinion is by its nature a matter of most significance, but it is described in the Basis for Qualified / Adverse Opinion section, with a reference in the KAM section.
- KAM explains areas of most significance in an audit where the auditor has reached a conclusion; it is not a separate opinion on individual matters.
- Hence the statement is incorrect.

questions.prompt: List the classes of companies to which CARO 2020 does not apply.
questions.answer:
- A banking company as defined in the Banking Regulation Act 1949.
- An insurance company as defined under the Insurance Act 1938.
- A company licensed to operate under section 8 of the Companies Act 2013.
- A One Person Company and a small company as defined in sections 2(62) and 2(85).
- A private limited company, not a holding or subsidiary of a public company, which: has paid-up capital and reserves and surplus not more than ₹1 crore as on the balance sheet date; does not have total borrowings exceeding ₹1 crore from any bank or financial institution at any point during the year; and does not have total revenue (including revenue from discontinuing operations) exceeding ₹10 crore during the year. All three must be met.
- CARO also does not apply to the report on consolidated FS, except clause 3(xxi).

chapters.title: Company Audit under the Companies Act 2013
chapters.summary: Eligibility, qualifications and disqualifications, appointment, rotation, removal, resignation, remuneration, rights and duties of company auditors under sections 139 to 148 of the Companies Act 2013, read with SA 210 on terms of engagement.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act 2013 (sections 139-148) and Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014 as amended up to 2026; SA 210

lesson.heading: Eligibility, qualifications and disqualifications (section 141)
lesson.body:
In the ICAI new scheme module this topic sits with 'Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements'. SA 210 requires the auditor to agree the terms of the engagement in an **engagement letter**; for companies, many terms are fixed by law.

**Eligible (s. 141(1), (2)):** a chartered accountant in practice, or a firm (including an LLP) whose majority of partners practising in India are CAs. When a firm is appointed, only partners who are CAs may act and sign.

**Not eligible (s. 141(3)), key items:**

| Clause | Disqualification |
| --- | --- |
| (a) | A body corporate other than an LLP |
| (b) | An officer or employee of the company |
| (c) | A partner or employee of an officer or employee of the company |
| (d)(i) | Person, relative or partner holding any security or interest in the company, its subsidiary, holding or associate company or subsidiary of its holding company. A relative may hold securities of face value up to ₹1,00,000 |
| (d)(ii) | Person, relative or partner indebted to the company or the above entities for more than ₹5,00,000 |
| (d)(iii) | Person, relative or partner who has given a guarantee or security for a third party's indebtedness to the company for more than ₹1,00,000 |
| (e) | A person or firm with a business relationship with the company or the above entities (other than in the ordinary course for commercial transactions at arm's length) |
| (f) | A person whose relative is a director or key managerial personnel |
| (g) | A person in full-time employment elsewhere, or a person or partner holding appointment as auditor of more than **20 companies** (excluding OPCs, dormant companies, small companies and private companies with paid-up capital below ₹100 crore) |
| (h) | A person convicted of an offence involving fraud, for 10 years from the conviction |
| (i) | A person or subsidiary / associate who is rendering services barred by section 144 |

If a disqualification arises after appointment, the auditor **vacates office** and it is a casual vacancy (s. 141(4)).

lesson.heading: Appointment (section 139)
lesson.body:
| Situation | Non-government company | Government company |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First auditor | Board within 30 days of registration; if Board fails, members at an EGM within 90 days. Holds office till the first AGM | CAG within 60 days of registration; if CAG fails, Board within next 30 days; if Board fails, members at an EGM within next 60 days |
| Subsequent auditor | Members at the first AGM appoint for a term from that AGM to the conclusion of the sixth AGM (5 years) | CAG within 180 days from the start of the financial year, till the next AGM |
| Casual vacancy | Board within 30 days; if caused by resignation, the Board's appointment must be approved by members at a general meeting within 3 months of the Board's recommendation. Holds office till the next AGM | CAG within 30 days; if CAG fails, Board within next 30 days |

The annual ratification of appointment at each AGM was omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2017 (effective 2018). The company must obtain the auditor's **written consent** and a certificate that he satisfies the criteria of section 141, and file **Form ADT-1** with the Registrar within 15 days of the meeting.

**Rotation (s. 139(2))** applies to listed companies and prescribed classes: unlisted public companies with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more; private companies with paid-up capital of ₹50 crore or more; and companies (other than those above) with public borrowings from financial institutions, banks or public deposits of ₹50 crore or more.

| Auditor | Maximum | Cooling-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Individual | One term of 5 consecutive years | 5 years |
| Audit firm (including LLP) | Two terms of 5 consecutive years (10 years) | 5 years |

During cooling-off, a firm with common partners cannot be appointed.

lesson.heading: Removal, resignation, retiring auditor and remuneration (sections 139-142)
lesson.body:
**Removal before expiry of term (s. 140(1)):** by **special resolution** after obtaining the **previous approval of the Central Government**. The Board passes a resolution and applies to the Central Government (Form ADT-2) within 30 days; the general meeting is held within 60 days of receiving approval. The auditor must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

**Resignation (s. 140(2)):** the auditor files a statement in **Form ADT-3** within 30 days of resigning with the company and the Registrar (and with the CAG for government companies), giving reasons and other facts.

**Appointing an auditor other than the retiring auditor (s. 140(4)):** a **special notice** is required for a resolution at an AGM appointing someone other than the retiring auditor or providing that the retiring auditor shall not be reappointed (except where he has completed his term under s. 139(2)). The retiring auditor may make written representations, which are sent to members or read at the meeting.

**Tribunal (s. 140(5)):** the NCLT may order a change of auditor if satisfied that the auditor acted fraudulently or abetted fraud; such an auditor cannot be appointed by any company for 5 years.

**Reappointment of retiring auditor (s. 139(9), (10)):** he may be reappointed if not disqualified, has not given written notice of unwillingness and no special resolution has been passed appointing someone else or barring his reappointment. If no auditor is appointed at the AGM, the existing auditor continues.

**Remuneration (s. 142):** fixed by the company in general meeting or as determined there; for the first auditor, the Board may fix it. It includes expenses incurred in connection with the audit but not fees for other permitted services.

lesson.heading: Rights, duties and prohibited services (sections 143-148)
lesson.body:
**Rights:**

- **Access** at all times to books, accounts and vouchers, wherever kept (s. 143(1)), including those of subsidiaries for the holding company auditor, for consolidation purposes.
- To require **information and explanations** from officers.
- To receive notices of, attend and be heard at **general meetings** (s. 146). The auditor must attend, himself or through an authorised representative qualified to be an auditor, unless exempted by the company.
- Branch audit: the company auditor may visit branches and access branch records and branch auditor's report (s. 143(8)).

**Duties:**

- **Inquire** into six matters under s. 143(1): loans and advances properly secured and on terms not prejudicial; book entries prejudicial to the company; sale of investments by a non-investment company at less than cost; loans and advances shown as deposits; personal expenses charged to revenue; shares allotted for cash where cash was not actually received.
- **Report** to members (s. 143(2), (3)) on whether FS give a true and fair view, and on matters such as information obtained, proper books, agreement with books, compliance with accounting standards, adverse effects of observations, director disqualification under s. 164(2), adequacy and operating effectiveness of internal financial controls, and other matters in Rule 11 (pending litigation, foreseeable losses, IEPF transfers, audit trail).
- Comply with **SAs** (s. 143(9), (10)) and CARO 2020 (s. 143(11)).
- **Report fraud (s. 143(12))**: fraud involving ₹1 crore or more by officers or employees is reported to the Central Government (Form ADT-4); below ₹1 crore, to the audit committee or Board, and the details are disclosed in the Board's report.

**Prohibited services (s. 144)**, directly or indirectly, to the company, its holding or subsidiary: accounting and book keeping; internal audit; design and implementation of any financial information system; actuarial services; investment advisory services; investment banking services; rendering of outsourced financial services; management services. Other permitted services need Board or audit committee approval.

lesson.heading: Answering company audit questions
lesson.body:
Structure: provision (section and sub-section), facts, conclusion. State numbers precisely (30 days, 90 days, 60 days, ₹5 lakh, ₹1 lakh, 20 companies, 5 / 10 years).

**Worked example.** CA Vikram's brother holds equity shares of face value ₹80,000 in X Ltd, where Vikram is to be appointed auditor. Under s. 141(3)(d)(i) read with Rule 10, a relative may hold securities of face value not exceeding ₹1,00,000. Vikram is **not disqualified**, though he must ensure the limit is not exceeded and act on any excess within the time allowed under the Rules.

**Common mistakes:**

- Saying the Board can remove an auditor (removal before the term needs a special resolution plus Central Government approval).
- Writing that appointment must be ratified every year (omitted from 2018).
- Applying rotation to every company; it applies to listed and prescribed classes only.
- Treating the ₹5 lakh indebtedness limit as applying to security holding.
- Forgetting that a firm is limited to two terms and an individual to one term.

keyPoints: s. 141(3): body corporate (other than LLP), officer or employee, relative security holding above ₹1 lakh face value, indebtedness above ₹5 lakh, guarantee above ₹1 lakh, relative as director or KMP, more than 20 company audits.
First auditor (non-government): Board within 30 days of registration; else members at EGM within 90 days.
Subsequent auditor: appointed at AGM for 5 years (first to sixth AGM); file ADT-1 within 15 days.
Rotation: individual one term of 5 years; firm two terms of 5 years; 5-year cooling-off.
Removal before term: special resolution plus prior Central Government approval; resignation: ADT-3 within 30 days.
s. 143(12): fraud of ₹1 crore or more to Central Government; below ₹1 crore to audit committee or Board.
s. 144: eight prohibited services including accounting, internal audit, FIS design, actuarial, investment advisory and banking, outsourced financial and management services.

cases.title: Case: Vardhan Infra Limited
cases.body:
Vardhan Infra Limited is an unlisted public company with paid-up share capital of ₹15 crore. It was incorporated on 1 April 2019. Facts:

- M/s Rao and Co. (a firm) was first appointed auditor in 2019 and is now serving its second five-year term.
- CA Sunil Rao, a partner of the firm, has taken a personal loan of ₹6,50,000 from Vardhan Infra Limited.
- The managing director wants to remove M/s Rao and Co. before its term ends by a simple Board resolution because they have raised questions on related party transactions.
- The company has asked M/s Rao and Co. to also take up the internal audit for FY 2027-28 at a separate fee.
- During the FY 2026-27 audit, the firm finds that the purchase manager has misappropriated ₹1,40,00,000 through fictitious vendors.

questions.prompt: The first auditor of a non-government company is appointed by the Board of Directors within:
questions.explanation: Section 139(6): the Board appoints the first auditor within 30 days of registration; if it fails, members appoint at an EGM within 90 days.

questions.prompt: A casual vacancy in the office of auditor of a non-government company caused by resignation is filled by:
options: The Board within 30 days, and the appointment must be approved by members at a general meeting within 3 months
The members at the next AGM only
questions.explanation: Section 139(8)(i): the Board fills a casual vacancy within 30 days; if caused by resignation, the company in general meeting must approve it within 3 months of the Board's recommendation.

questions.prompt: An auditor who resigns must file a statement in which form within 30 days?
questions.explanation: ADT-1 is notice of appointment, ADT-2 is the application for removal, ADT-3 is the resignation statement and ADT-4 is the fraud report to the Central Government.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT disqualified from being appointed auditor of a company under section 141?
options: A body corporate other than an LLP
A CA whose relative holds shares of the company of face value ₹60,000
A CA whose relative is a director of the company
questions.explanation: A relative may hold securities of face value up to ₹1,00,000 (Rule 10). The others are disqualified under section 141(3)(a), (b) and (f).

questions.prompt: Is CA Sunil Rao's loan of ₹6,50,000 from the company a problem?
options: No, loans are allowed up to ₹10,00,000
Yes; a partner indebted to the company for more than ₹5,00,000 disqualifies the firm under section 141(3)(d)(ii), so it must vacate office
No, because the loan is personal and not the firm's
Yes, but only CA Sunil Rao is barred from signing
questions.explanation: Section 141(3)(d)(ii) covers indebtedness of the person, relative or partner above ₹5 lakh. Under section 141(4), a disqualification after appointment causes the auditor to vacate office.

questions.prompt: Can the managing director remove M/s Rao and Co. by a Board resolution?
options: Yes, the Board can remove the auditor at any time
No; removal before expiry of term needs a special resolution with the previous approval of the Central Government, after giving the auditor an opportunity of being heard
Yes, with an ordinary resolution of members
No, an auditor can never be removed before the term ends
questions.explanation: Section 140(1) requires a special resolution after Central Government approval (ADT-2 within 30 days of the Board resolution).

questions.prompt: May M/s Rao and Co. accept the internal audit assignment?
options: Yes, with approval of the Board
Yes, if the fee is less than the statutory audit fee
No; internal audit is a service the company auditor cannot render under section 144
Yes, because the company is unlisted
questions.explanation: Section 144 prohibits the auditor from providing internal audit services to the company, its holding or subsidiary company, directly or indirectly.

questions.prompt: How should the firm report the ₹1,40,00,000 misappropriation by the purchase manager?
options: To the audit committee only, since the amount is below ₹2 crore
To the Central Government under section 143(12), since the fraud is ₹1 crore or more
No reporting is required as management will handle it
questions.explanation: Fraud of ₹1 crore or more by officers or employees is reported to the Central Government in Form ADT-4 under section 143(12). It is also reported under CARO clause 3(xi).

questions.prompt: Rotation applies to Vardhan Infra Limited. Counting from its first appointment in 2019, what is the maximum number of consecutive years M/s Rao and Co. can serve before the cooling-off period?
questions.explanation: An unlisted public company with paid-up capital of ₹10 crore or more is a prescribed class under section 139(2). An audit firm may serve two terms of five consecutive years = 10 years, then a 5-year cooling-off.

questions.prompt: Under the Companies Act 2013 as amended, the appointment of the auditor must be ratified by members at every AGM.
questions.explanation: The ratification requirement in the first proviso to section 139(1) was omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2017 with effect from 2018.

questions.prompt: An LLP of chartered accountants can be appointed as the auditor of a company.
questions.explanation: Section 141(1) allows a firm, including an LLP, whose majority of partners practising in India are qualified for appointment. Section 141(3)(a) excludes body corporates other than LLPs.

questions.prompt: Which of the following services are prohibited for a company auditor under section 144? (Select all that apply.)
options: Design and implementation of any financial information system
Tax audit under the Income-tax law
questions.explanation: Section 144 lists eight prohibited services. Tax audit is not listed, though the auditor must get Board or audit committee approval for other permitted services.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: A person who is auditor of more than ___ companies (excluding the exempted classes) is disqualified under section 141(3)(g).
questions.explanation: The ceiling is 20 companies, excluding OPCs, dormant companies, small companies and private companies with paid-up capital below ₹100 crore.

questions.prompt: State the disqualifications of a company auditor under section 141(3) of the Companies Act 2013.
questions.answer:
- (a) A body corporate other than an LLP.
- (b) An officer or employee of the company.
- (c) A person who is a partner, or in employment, of an officer or employee of the company.
- (d) A person who, or whose relative or partner: holds any security or interest in the company, its subsidiary, holding or associate company or subsidiary of its holding company (relative may hold up to ₹1 lakh face value); is indebted to any of them above ₹5 lakh; or has given a guarantee or security for a third person's indebtedness to them above ₹1 lakh.
- (e) A person or firm with a direct or indirect business relationship with them, other than ordinary-course arm's length commercial transactions.
- (f) A person whose relative is a director or key managerial personnel.
- (g) A person in full-time employment elsewhere, or holding appointment as auditor of more than 20 companies (excluding exempt classes).
- (h) A person convicted of an offence involving fraud, for 10 years from conviction.
- (i) A person or its subsidiary / associate rendering services barred by section 144.
- If a disqualification arises after appointment, the auditor vacates office (s. 141(4)).

questions.prompt: Explain the provisions for removal of an auditor before the expiry of the term and for appointing an auditor other than the retiring auditor.
questions.answer:
- Section 140(1): the auditor may be removed before expiry of the term only by a special resolution, after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government.
- Rule 7: the Board passes a resolution and applies to the Central Government in Form ADT-2 within 30 days; the general meeting is held within 60 days of receiving approval.
- The auditor must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
- Section 140(4): special notice is required for a resolution at an AGM appointing a person other than the retiring auditor, or providing that the retiring auditor shall not be reappointed (except where his term under s. 139(2) is over).
- The company sends a copy of the notice to the retiring auditor, who may make written representations; these are sent to members, or read at the meeting if received late.
- Section 140(5): the NCLT may order a change if the auditor acted fraudulently; such an auditor is barred for 5 years.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'The company auditor can refuse to attend the general meeting since his report is already sent to members.'
questions.answer:
- Not correct.
- Section 146 entitles the auditor to receive all notices of general meetings and to attend and be heard on any part of the business that concerns him as auditor.
- It also requires the auditor, unless exempted by the company, to attend the general meeting either himself or through an authorised representative who is qualified to be an auditor.
- Attendance allows members to seek clarifications on the audit report and the auditor to explain qualifications.
- Hence the auditor cannot refuse unless the company has exempted him.
