chapters.title: Audit of Banks and Audit of Different Types of Entities
chapters.summary: Basics of bank audit (appointment, approach, advances, NPA identification and income recognition) and special features of audits of government entities, local bodies, NGOs and cooperative societies.
chapters.lawAsOf: Banking Regulation Act 1949; RBI prudential norms on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning (IRACP) as in force in 2026; Constitution of India Articles 148-151 and CAG (DPC) Act 1971; state cooperative laws and Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act 2002

lesson.heading: Bank audit: framework and approach
lesson.body:
**Legal framework:** banking companies prepare financial statements under **section 29** of the Banking Regulation Act 1949 in the forms in the Third Schedule (Form A balance sheet, Form B profit and loss account). Under **section 30**, the accounts are audited by a person qualified to be an auditor of companies, appointed with the **previous approval of the RBI**. Public sector banks appoint statutory central auditors and branch auditors under their own statutes, also with RBI approval.

**Structure:** **Statutory Central Auditors (SCAs)** audit head office and report on the bank as a whole; **branch auditors** audit selected branches and report to the SCAs. Besides the main report, auditors give a **Long Form Audit Report (LFAR)** in the format prescribed by the RBI, covering detailed observations on advances, deposits, controls and compliance.

**Approach:**

- Understand the bank's systems: **Core Banking Solution (CBS)**, treasury, credit appraisal, concurrent and internal audit reports, RBI inspection reports.
- Assess risk: advances (credit risk), treasury, frauds, IT access.
- Rely on controls where appropriate (system-driven NPA tagging) but verify through sample testing.
- Areas: cash and balances with RBI, balances with banks, investments, **advances**, deposits, other liabilities, interest income and expenses, contingent liabilities (guarantees, letters of credit).

lesson.heading: Advances, NPAs and income recognition
lesson.body:
Advances are the most significant area. The auditor checks sanction, documentation, security, disbursement, end use, monitoring, drawing power and classification.

**Non-performing asset (NPA)** under RBI IRACP norms: a loan or advance where:

| Facility | NPA when |
| --- | --- |
| Term loan | Interest and / or instalment of principal remains **overdue for more than 90 days** |
| Overdraft / cash credit | Account remains **'out of order'** (outstanding continuously above sanctioned limit or drawing power for 90 days, or no credits continuously for 90 days, or credits not enough to cover interest debited) |
| Bills purchased and discounted | Bill remains overdue for more than 90 days |
| Agricultural advances, short duration crops | Instalment or interest overdue for **two crop seasons** |
| Agricultural advances, long duration crops | Overdue for **one crop season** |

**Asset classification:**

| Category | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Standard | Not NPA |
| Sub-standard | NPA for a period up to 12 months |
| Doubtful | Remained sub-standard for 12 months |
| Loss | Loss identified by the bank, auditors or RBI inspection but not written off wholly |

**Income recognition:** interest on NPAs is recognised only when **actually received** (realisation basis), not on accrual. Interest accrued and credited to income in an earlier period that remains unrealised when the account turns NPA should be reversed.

Classification is **borrower-wise**, not facility-wise: if one facility of a borrower is NPA, all facilities of that borrower are NPA.

Note: the RBI has been moving toward an expected credit loss framework for provisioning. Check the latest ICAI study material for any change in provisioning content for your attempt.

lesson.heading: Government audit and local bodies
lesson.body:
**Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG):** Articles 148 to 151 of the Constitution and the CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act 1971. The CAG audits receipts and expenditure of the Union and states, government companies (by appointing auditors and conducting supplementary audit) and bodies substantially financed by government. CAG reports are laid before Parliament or state legislatures.

**Kinds of government audit:**

| Type | Checks |
| --- | --- |
| Audit against provision of funds | Expenditure covered by appropriation approved by the legislature |
| Audit against rules and orders (regularity) | Expenditure conforms to rules, regulations and orders |
| Audit of sanctions | Expenditure has sanction of the competent authority |
| Propriety audit | Expenditure is wise, faithful and economical; no extravagance; not for the benefit of a particular person |
| Performance audit | Economy, efficiency and effectiveness of programmes |

**Local bodies** (municipal corporations, municipalities, panchayats) are audited under state laws, usually by the Examiner / Director of Local Fund Audit, with chartered accountants appointed in some states; the CAG provides technical guidance and supervision. Focus: budget compliance, property tax and other receipts, grants utilisation, works contracts, and expenditure sanctions.

lesson.heading: NGOs and cooperative societies
lesson.body:
**NGOs** may be trusts, societies (Societies Registration Act 1860) or section 8 companies. Special points:

- Read the constitution documents (trust deed, bye-laws) for objects and powers.
- Verify **grants**: agreements, conditions, utilisation for stated purposes, unspent balances, utilisation certificates.
- **Foreign contribution**: check compliance with the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010, including receipt only in the designated FCRA account and separate books.
- Donations: controls over receipts, issue of receipts, cash donations.
- Income-tax exemption conditions for charitable entities (application of income, registration).
- Expenses: approval, payments to related persons, administrative expense ratios.

**Cooperative societies** are audited under the state Co-operative Societies Act (or the **Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act 2002** for multi-state societies), usually by auditors on a panel approved by the Registrar or appointed by the general body as the law provides. Special features:

- Verify compliance with the Act, Rules and bye-laws.
- Examine overdue loans to members, their recovery and adequacy of provisions.
- Check that interest and dividends are within limits, and reserve fund transfers are made as required.
- Report in the form prescribed by the Registrar, including an **audit classification** (grading such as A, B, C, D) based on performance.
- Report misappropriation, irregularities and recoverable amounts to the Registrar.

**Common mistakes:** applying company law rules to cooperative and trust audits; ignoring grant conditions; calling regularity audit 'propriety audit'.

keyPoints: Bank accounts: section 29 BR Act, Third Schedule Forms A and B; section 30 audit with prior RBI approval.
SCAs report on the bank as a whole; branch auditors report to SCAs; LFAR in RBI format.
Term loan NPA: overdue more than 90 days; CC/OD NPA when out of order for 90 days.
Agriculture: short duration crops two crop seasons; long duration crops one crop season.
Sub-standard up to 12 months as NPA; doubtful after 12 months as sub-standard; loss when identified but not written off.
Interest on NPAs recognised on realisation; classification is borrower-wise.
Government audit types: provision of funds, regularity, sanctions, propriety, performance (CAG, Articles 148-151).

cases.title: Case: Branch audit of Narmada Bank, Indore branch
cases.body:
CA Kiran Joshi is the branch auditor of the Indore branch of Narmada Bank Limited for the year ended 31 March 2027. Selected accounts:

| Borrower | Facility | Position at 31 March 2027 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shree Polymers | Term loan of ₹2,40,00,000 | Instalment due on 15 December 2026 unpaid |
| Shree Polymers | Cash credit of ₹80,00,000 | Regular, within drawing power |
| Patel Traders | Cash credit, limit ₹50,00,000 | Outstanding above drawing power continuously since 10 November 2026 |
| Ramesh Patil (farmer) | Crop loan for wheat (short duration crop) | One crop season overdue |

The branch has credited interest of ₹9,60,000 on the Shree Polymers term loan to income for the quarter January-March 2027, none of which has been received.

questions.prompt: Under section 30 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949, the auditor of a banking company is appointed:
options: By the bank with the previous approval of the Reserve Bank of India
questions.explanation: Section 30 requires audit by a person qualified to be a company auditor, appointed with the prior approval of the RBI.

questions.prompt: An asset that has remained in the sub-standard category for 12 months is classified as:
questions.explanation: Under IRACP norms, a doubtful asset is one that has remained sub-standard for 12 months.

questions.prompt: Examining whether expenditure was wise, faithful and economical, and not for the benefit of a particular person, is called:
questions.explanation: Propriety audit looks beyond legality to public interest and prudence. Regularity audit checks compliance with rules and orders.

questions.prompt: While auditing an NGO that receives foreign donations, the auditor should specifically check compliance with:
options: The Foreign Exchange Management Act only
The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010, including receipt in the designated FCRA account
questions.explanation: Foreign contributions to NGOs are governed by FCRA 2010, which requires receipt in the designated account and separate records.

questions.prompt: For how many days was the Shree Polymers term loan instalment overdue as on 31 March 2027? (Count from the day after the due date, including 31 March.)
questions.explanation:
| Period | Days |
| --- | --- |
| 16-31 December 2026 | 16 |
| January 2027 | 31 |
| February 2027 | 28 |
| March 2027 | 31 |
| **Total** | **106** |

Since 106 exceeds 90 days, the term loan is an NPA.

questions.prompt: How should Shree Polymers' cash credit account (which is regular) be classified?
options: NPA, because classification is borrower-wise and the term loan of the same borrower is NPA
questions.explanation: Asset classification is borrower-wise. If any facility of a borrower is NPA, all facilities of that borrower are classified as NPA.

questions.prompt: What should Kiran recommend for the ₹9,60,000 unrealised interest on the Shree Polymers term loan?
options: Retain it in income since it is legally due
Reverse it from income, as interest on NPAs is recognised only on realisation
questions.explanation: IRACP norms require income on NPAs to be recognised on realisation. Unrealised interest credited to income must be reversed.

questions.prompt: Which accounts in the case are NPAs as on 31 March 2027? (Select all that apply.)
questions.explanation: Term loan: overdue 106 days. Shree Polymers CC: borrower-wise. Patel Traders: above drawing power continuously for more than 90 days (10 November 2026 to 31 March 2027 is 141 days), so out of order. A short duration crop loan becomes NPA only after two crop seasons overdue; one season is not enough.

questions.prompt: A crop loan for a long duration crop becomes an NPA if the instalment or interest remains overdue for one crop season.
questions.explanation: IRACP norms: long duration crops one crop season; short duration crops two crop seasons.

questions.prompt: Performance audit by the CAG examines only whether expenditure was covered by legislative appropriation.
questions.explanation: That describes audit against provision of funds. Performance audit examines economy, efficiency and effectiveness of programmes and schemes.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Besides the main audit report, bank auditors submit a ___ Form Audit Report (LFAR) in the format prescribed by the RBI.
questions.explanation: The LFAR covers detailed observations on advances, deposits, internal controls and compliance.

questions.prompt: How will you verify advances during the audit of a bank branch?
questions.answer:
- Obtain branch-wise advance balances and reconcile with the general ledger and CBS reports.
- Examine sanction: proposals, appraisal, sanction by the competent authority within delegated powers.
- Check documentation: loan agreements, hypothecation and mortgage documents, guarantees, registration of charges where needed, and their validity.
- Verify security: stock statements, drawing power calculations, inspection reports, valuation reports and insurance.
- Review monitoring: renewals, overdrawn accounts, irregularities and end use of funds.
- Classify accounts under IRACP norms (90-day overdue / out of order, crop seasons, borrower-wise) and test system-generated NPA tagging.
- Check income recognition: interest on NPAs on realisation; reverse unrealised interest.
- Check provisions and disclosures, and report in the LFAR and to SCAs.

questions.prompt: Explain the kinds of audit conducted by the CAG in government departments.
questions.answer:
- Audit against provision of funds: expenditure is within the appropriation authorised by Parliament or the state legislature.
- Audit against rules and orders (regularity): expenditure conforms to the Constitution, laws, rules and orders.
- Audit of sanctions: every item of expenditure has sanction (general or special) of the competent authority.
- Propriety audit: expenditure is wise, faithful and economical, not excessive, and not for the benefit of a particular person or section.
- Performance audit: whether programmes achieve objectives with economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
- Authority: Articles 148-151 of the Constitution and the CAG (DPC) Act 1971; reports are laid before the legislature.

questions.prompt: State the special points the auditor should consider in the audit of a cooperative society.
questions.answer:
- Applicable law: the state Co-operative Societies Act and Rules, or the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act 2002, and the society's bye-laws.
- Appointment as per the law (often from a panel approved by the Registrar or by the general body).
- Compliance with the Act, Rules and bye-laws: membership, share capital, borrowing limits, investments.
- Loans to members: sanction, security, overdue loans, recovery steps and provisions.
- Appropriation of profits: statutory reserve fund transfer, dividend limits.
- Verification of assets and liabilities, and transactions with members and directors.
- Report in the prescribed form to the Registrar, including the audit classification (grading), irregularities, misappropriations and amounts recoverable.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'A bank may continue to book interest on an NPA account on accrual basis if the security is adequate.'
questions.answer:
- Not correct.
- Under RBI prudential norms on income recognition, income from NPAs is recognised only when actually received, since it is not realised.
- Adequacy of security does not change this; it affects provisioning, not income recognition.
- Interest accrued and credited to income earlier that is unrealised when the account becomes NPA should be reversed.
- The auditor checks that the system stops accrual on NPA accounts and that reversals are made.
- Hence the statement is incorrect.

chapters.title: Professional Ethics and Code of Ethics
chapters.summary: Fundamental principles, threats and safeguards under the ICAI Code of Ethics, independence of the auditor, and the basics of professional misconduct under the First and Second Schedules to the Chartered Accountants Act 1949.
chapters.lawAsOf: ICAI Code of Ethics (current edition) and the Chartered Accountants Act 1949 as amended by the Chartered Accountants (Amendment) Act 2022

lesson.heading: Fundamental principles and the conceptual framework
lesson.body:
The ICAI **Code of Ethics** requires every member to comply with five **fundamental principles**:

| Principle | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Integrity | Be straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships |
| Objectivity | Do not compromise judgment because of bias, conflict of interest or undue influence |
| Professional competence and due care | Keep knowledge and skill current; act diligently per technical and professional standards |
| Confidentiality | Respect confidentiality of information acquired in professional relationships; no disclosure without authority unless a legal or professional right or duty exists; no use for personal advantage |
| Professional behaviour | Comply with laws and regulations and avoid conduct that discredits the profession |

The Code uses a **conceptual framework approach**: the member must **identify** threats to compliance with the principles, **evaluate** whether they are at an acceptable level and **address** them by eliminating the circumstances, applying safeguards or declining / ending the engagement.

**Independence** for assurance engagements has two parts: **independence of mind** (state of mind allowing an opinion without influence) and **independence in appearance** (avoiding facts and circumstances so significant that a reasonable and informed third party would conclude integrity or objectivity is compromised).

lesson.heading: Threats and safeguards
lesson.body:
| Threat | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Self-interest | Financial or other interest inappropriately influences judgment | Auditor holds shares in the client; undue dependence on fees from one client; contingent fee |
| Self-review | Member evaluates his own previous work | Auditor prepares the accounts or designs the financial information system he then audits |
| Advocacy | Member promotes the client's position to the point that objectivity is compromised | Auditor represents the client in a dispute with a third party, or promotes its shares |
| Familiarity | Long or close relationship makes the member too sympathetic | Long association of a senior partner; close relative in a key position at the client |
| Intimidation | Member is deterred from acting objectively by actual or perceived pressure | Threat of dismissal or litigation; pressure to reduce work to cut fees |

**Safeguards** include: involving an additional professional to review work; using separate teams for non-audit services; rotating senior personnel; disclosure to those charged with governance; obtaining client approval; declining the engagement when no safeguard reduces the threat to an acceptable level.

For company audits, section 144 (prohibited services) and section 141 (disqualifications) of the Companies Act 2013 are statutory responses to self-review and self-interest threats.

lesson.heading: Professional misconduct: CA Act 1949 schedules (basics)
lesson.body:
The Chartered Accountants Act 1949 lists acts of professional and other misconduct in two Schedules. Complaints go to the **Director (Discipline)**; matters only under the First Schedule are heard by the **Board of Discipline**, and matters under the Second Schedule or both Schedules by the **Disciplinary Committee**.

**First Schedule, Part I (members in practice), selected clauses:** a member in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he:

| Clause | Act |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Allows any person to practise in his name as a CA unless that person is a CA in practice and is his partner or employee |
| 2 | Pays or allows a share, commission or brokerage in his fees to anyone other than a member, partner or retired partner, or legal representative of a deceased partner |
| 4 | Enters into partnership with a person other than a CA in practice (or a person permitted by the Council) |
| 6 | Solicits clients or professional work, directly or indirectly, by circular, advertisement, personal communication or interview or any other means (with exceptions permitted by the Council) |
| 7 | Advertises his professional attainments or services, or uses any designation other than CA on professional documents and visiting cards (with Council-permitted exceptions) |
| 8 | Accepts a position as auditor previously held by another CA without first communicating with him in writing |
| 9 | Accepts appointment as auditor of a company without first ascertaining that the requirements of the Companies Act relating to appointment have been duly complied with |
| 10 | Charges or offers to charge fees based on a percentage of profits or contingent on findings or results (except as permitted by regulations) |
| 11 | Engages in any business or occupation other than the profession of CA unless permitted by the Council |
| 12 | Allows a person who is not a member in practice, or a member who is not his partner, to sign on his behalf or on behalf of his firm any balance sheet, profit and loss account or report on financial statements |

**Second Schedule, Part I (members in practice), selected clauses:** guilty if he:

| Clause | Act |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Discloses information acquired in professional engagement to anyone other than the client without consent, except as required by law |
| 2 | Certifies or submits a report on financial statements unless he, his partner or employee examined them |
| 4 | Expresses his opinion on financial statements of a business in which he, his firm or a partner has a substantial interest |
| 5 | Fails to disclose a material fact known to him that is not disclosed in the financial statements, where necessary to make them not misleading |
| 6 | Fails to report a material misstatement known to him to appear in the financial statements |
| 7 | Does not exercise due diligence, or is grossly negligent in conducting professional duties |
| 8 | Fails to obtain sufficient information to warrant expressing an opinion, or his exceptions are sufficiently material to negate the opinion |
| 9 | Fails to invite attention to any material departure from generally accepted procedures of audit |
| 10 | Fails to keep moneys of his client in a separate bank account or to use them for the purposes intended |

The depth of CA Act content expected at Intermediate under the new scheme should be confirmed against the current ICAI study material.

lesson.heading: Answering ethics questions
lesson.body:
Use this frame: (1) state the relevant clause and schedule, or the Code principle and threat; (2) apply to facts; (3) conclude 'guilty / not guilty of professional misconduct under Clause (x) of Part I of the First Schedule'.

**Worked example.** CA Nidhi accepts appointment as auditor of a private company, replacing CA Mohan, without communicating with him. She argues the company's board resolution was valid. Under Clause (8) of Part I of the First Schedule, a member must communicate in writing with the previous auditor before accepting. Communication is a professional courtesy and lets the incoming auditor learn of any professional reasons not to accept. Nidhi is **guilty** of professional misconduct.

**Common mistakes:**

- Citing the wrong schedule (soliciting and advertising are First Schedule; disclosure of client information and gross negligence are Second Schedule).
- Treating the fee-sharing ban as covering fees shared with a partner who is a CA (it is permitted).
- Treating every non-audit service as prohibited; only section 144 services are barred for company audit clients.
- Ignoring independence in appearance.

keyPoints: Five fundamental principles: integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality, professional behaviour.
Conceptual framework: identify, evaluate and address threats.
Five threats: self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity, intimidation.
Independence of mind and independence in appearance.
First Schedule Part I: clause 6 soliciting, 7 advertising, 8 communicate with previous auditor in writing, 10 contingent / percentage fees, 12 allowing a non-partner to sign.
Second Schedule Part I: clause 1 confidentiality, 4 substantial interest, 7 gross negligence, 8 insufficient information, 10 client money in separate account.
Board of Discipline hears First Schedule matters; Disciplinary Committee hears Second Schedule or both.

cases.title: Case: CA Ankit Bansal
cases.body:
CA Ankit Bansal runs a proprietary practice. During 2026-27:

- He posts on social media: 'Best audit results guaranteed! 200+ satisfied clients, call now for a free consultation.'
- He accepts appointment as auditor of Kaveri Foods Private Limited, replacing CA Deepa, after a phone call with the company's director but without writing to CA Deepa.
- He agrees with a client to charge 2% of the tax refund obtained as his fee for representing it before the income-tax authorities.
- He pays 10% of his audit fee from clients introduced by Mr. Raj, a property broker (not a CA), as 'referral commission'.
- He discusses the confidential expansion plans of a client with a competitor of that client at a social gathering, without the client's consent.

questions.prompt: An auditor who also prepared the client's financial statements and then audits them faces mainly which threat?
questions.explanation: Evaluating his own previous work is a self-review threat. Section 144 also bars company auditors from accounting and book keeping services.

questions.prompt: A client threatens to replace the auditor unless he agrees with an aggressive accounting treatment. This is a:
questions.explanation: Actual or perceived pressure deterring the auditor from acting objectively is an intimidation threat.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the fundamental principles in the ICAI Code of Ethics?
questions.explanation: The five principles are integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality and professional behaviour.

questions.prompt: Matters of professional misconduct falling only under the First Schedule are heard by:
questions.explanation: Under the CA Act, the Board of Discipline deals with First Schedule matters; the Disciplinary Committee deals with Second Schedule matters or both Schedules.

questions.prompt: Ankit's social media post claiming guaranteed results and inviting calls is professional misconduct under:
options: Clauses (6) and (7) of Part I of the First Schedule (soliciting and advertising)
Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule
Clause (10) of Part I of the First Schedule
No clause, since social media is personal
questions.explanation: Soliciting work by advertisement and advertising professional attainments are barred by Clauses (6) and (7), subject only to Council-permitted exceptions. Guaranteeing results also breaches professional behaviour.

questions.prompt: Accepting the audit of Kaveri Foods without writing to CA Deepa is misconduct under:
options: Clause (8) of Part I of the First Schedule
Clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule
Clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule
No clause, since a phone call with the director is enough
questions.explanation: Clause (8) requires the incoming auditor to communicate in writing with the previous auditor before accepting. A call with the client's director does not satisfy it.

questions.prompt: Paying 10% of fees to Mr. Raj, a property broker, as referral commission is misconduct under:
options: Clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule (sharing fees with a non-member) and possibly Clause (5) (securing work through a non-member)
Clause (9) of Part I of the Second Schedule
Clause (11) of Part I of the First Schedule only
No misconduct, as the payment is disclosed in his books
questions.explanation: Clause (2) bars sharing fees with anyone other than a member, partner, retired partner or legal representative of a deceased partner. Clause (5) bars securing professional business through a non-member.

questions.prompt: Discussing the client's confidential expansion plans with a competitor without consent makes Ankit guilty under Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule.
questions.explanation: Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule covers disclosure of information acquired in the course of professional engagement without the client's consent or legal requirement. It also breaches the confidentiality principle.

questions.prompt: A CA in practice may share his fees with a partner who is a chartered accountant in practice.
questions.explanation: Clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule permits sharing fees with a member, a partner or retired partner, or the legal representative of a deceased partner.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are threats to compliance with the fundamental principles under the Code of Ethics? (Select all that apply.)
questions.explanation: The five threats are self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity and intimidation. Materiality is an audit concept, not a threat category.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Matters of professional misconduct under the Second Schedule, or under both Schedules, are heard by the ___ Committee.
questions.explanation: The Disciplinary Committee hears Second Schedule matters and matters under both Schedules.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons on Ankit's agreement to charge 2% of the tax refund obtained as his fee.
questions.answer:
- Clause (10) of Part I of the First Schedule bars a member in practice from charging or offering to charge fees based on a percentage of profits or contingent upon the findings or results of the work, except as permitted under the regulations framed by the Council.
- Fees as a percentage of a tax refund depend on the result of his work, so they are contingent fees.
- This also creates a self-interest threat to objectivity under the Code of Ethics.
- Unless the specific assignment falls within an exception permitted by the regulations (it does not for representation before tax authorities), Ankit is guilty of professional misconduct under Clause (10).

questions.prompt: Explain the five fundamental principles of professional ethics under the ICAI Code of Ethics.
questions.answer:
- Integrity: be straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships; do not be associated with false or misleading information.
- Objectivity: do not allow bias, conflict of interest or undue influence to override professional judgment.
- Professional competence and due care: maintain knowledge and skill so clients receive competent service, and act diligently in line with technical and professional standards.
- Confidentiality: do not disclose information acquired in professional relationships without proper authority unless there is a legal or professional right or duty, and do not use it for personal advantage.
- Professional behaviour: comply with relevant laws and regulations and avoid actions that discredit the profession.
- Threats to these are identified, evaluated and addressed under the conceptual framework.

questions.prompt: Explain the threats to independence with examples and state safeguards that may reduce them.
questions.answer:
- Self-interest: financial interest in the client, undue fee dependence, loans from the client, contingent fees.
- Self-review: preparing accounts or designing systems later audited; a former employee of the client auditing his own earlier work.
- Advocacy: promoting the client's shares or acting as its advocate in disputes.
- Familiarity: long association of senior personnel; a close relative in a senior position at the client; accepting significant gifts.
- Intimidation: threat of replacement, litigation or pressure to reduce audit work.
- Safeguards: independent review by another professional; rotation of senior team members; separate teams for non-audit services; communication with those charged with governance; obtaining approvals; declining or withdrawing where no safeguard reduces the threat to an acceptable level.
- For company audits, sections 141 and 144 of the Companies Act 2013 add statutory safeguards.

questions.prompt: Comment with reasons: 'A chartered accountant in practice may allow his senior article assistant to sign the audit report on his behalf when he is out of town.'
questions.answer:
- Not correct.
- Clause (12) of Part I of the First Schedule makes a member in practice guilty of professional misconduct if he allows a person who is not a member in practice, or a member who is not his partner, to sign on his behalf or on behalf of his firm any balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements.
- An article assistant is not a member in practice, so the CA cannot allow the assistant to sign.
- The signing authority stays with the member or a partner of the firm, who must also have examined or supervised the examination (Clause (2) of Part I of the Second Schedule).
- Hence the statement is incorrect.
